#808. How David Leitch Made ‘How to Rob a Bank’ on a Budget — and Around Nicholas Hoult’s Torn ACL

The action filmmaker moved fast — and got creative — to shoot the movie in half the days of his previous movie, 'The Fall Guy,' all with an injured leading man.

Director David Leitch has spent his career designing high-octane action for audiences to enjoy on the big screen. How to Rob a Bank, his sixth feature film since co-directing John Wick, is the first he’s made to inspire audiences to take action themselves.

At a certain point in How to Rob a Bank, the fourth wall is broken to deliver a shot across the bow to those in power: Either fix the broken economic system, or we’ll fix it for you. Nov. 3rd’s midterm elections were Americans’ way of pursuing the latter and taking matters into their own hands by electing candidates who prioritized combating the rising cost of living. Related Stories TV Nicholas Hoult Boards 'Harry Potter' Season 2 as Gilderoy Lockhart Movies 'Jason Statham Stole My Bike': David Leitch's Action-Comedy Sets Summer 2027 Release

When The Hollywood Reporter caught up with Leitch last month ahead of the midterms, the filmmaker remained optimistic that economic policies, both macro and micro, could still be corrected, starting at the ballot box.

“How to Rob a Bank challenges individuals to change the system. [Our protagonists] are asking you to be proactive in the ways that you can. Go out and vote for what you believe in. We still live in a democracy,” Leitch told The Hollywood Reporter on Oct. 5 in support of How to Rob a Bank’s Nov. 13 theatrical release. “I hope How to Rob a Bank is empowering and inspiring to people.”

The heist dramedy follows a crew of altruistic bank robbers who document their exploits on social media, hoping to galvanize others who share their belief that the American Dream has been hijacked by predatory, merciless institutions.

Led by Nicholas Hoult’s charismatic “The Wolf,” the masked gang behind the wildly popular YouTube channel Who’s Hungry? soon finds itself in the crosshairs of a frustrated FBI agent (John C. Reilly) and his newest ace in the hole, a criminal programmer (Zoë Kravitz) who agrees to help unmask the Robin Hood-esque thieves in exchange for her release from house arrest.

Considering that the film is produced and distributed by Amazon MGM, it’s worth noting that its parent company, the world’s largest by revenue, made no attempt to temper the film’s late-stage anti-capitalist stance.

“The filmmaking core at Amazon MGM are just trying to make great films that have all different types of messages,” Leitch says. “They want things to be provocative, and they want to encourage artists to speak their mind. So there was never any pushback from the studio about what we were making.”

For a film that wasn’t originally scripted to take place in the blue-collar city of Pittsburgh, it became the most Pittsburgh movie since The Dark Knight Rises, only more so since it shot Pittsburgh for Pittsburgh, not Gotham City. The production reportedly poured nearly $60 million into the Steel City’s local economy to qualify for a tax incentive. Still, Leitch describes the film as a relatively modest undertaking compared to his previous feature, The Fall Guy, which carried an estimated budget of $125 million to $150 million.

“We shot this in 40 days, and just to give you context, The Fall Guy was 86 days. So How to Rob a Bank is half the size of that film, and we just had to move quicker,” Leitch shares.

To make the most of those limited shooting days, Leitch deployed a second unit he dubbed the “YouTube unit,” made up primarily of stunt performers tasked with capturing the masked robbery sequences. This allowed Leitch and his ensemble — Hoult, Kravitz, Anna Sawai, Pete Davidson, Rhenzy Feliz, Reilly, and Christian Slater — to concentrate on the characters’ personal lives and the surprisingly dramatic territory the film gradually explores.

To distinguish the world of the anonymous YouTube characters from the real lives of the people behind them, Leitch and his team shot the in-universe videos on prosumer digital cameras, while the unmasked drama was filmed on 35mm film. Given the original film’s mid-budget constraints, Leitch acknowledges that the celluloid format required “a lot of number crunching.”

The second unit of masked stunt performers also proved particularly valuable in light of Hoult’s major injury at the time. Shortly before production began, the English actor tore his ACL while playing basketball. Rather than undergo surgery and drop out of the pic, he committed to intensive physical therapy three times a week to prepare for the demands of How to Rob a Bank. Leitch and his producing partner/wife, Kelly McCormick, nevertheless spared him considerable physical pain by structuring the shoot as they did.

But working around bad knees is old hat for Leitch, thanks to his background in the stunt department. Even Keanu Reeves dealt with a bum knee on the first John Wick — and, for that matter, throughout much of the franchise.

Below, during a conversation with THR, Leitch also discusses his next film, Jason Statham Stole My Bike, starring, you guessed it, Jason Statham.

Since John Wick, you’ve shot seven films, but you’ve been attached to at least a dozen more movies in development. How did How to Rob a Bank overtake everything else you’ve been juggling?

I love to find action genres and put my own spin on them and turn them on their head. I got to do it in the superhero genre with Deadpool 2. I got to do it in Atomic Blonde where we took a noir and made it a neon noir. I also got to do a romantic comedy with The Fall Guy. But I hadn’t done a heist movie. And when we read the script for How to Rob a Bank, I got really excited about how contemporary it was. It had this social media component, this content creator idea, that was so strong and interesting. Then it had these really grounded characters who were dealing with very timely issues that a lot of people are dealing with right now. So it just felt undeniable, and it moved to the top of the list very quickly.

How to Rob a Bank is a David-versus-Goliath story with an anti-capitalist message, and yet it’s being distributed by Amazon, the largest company in the world by annual revenue. Did they ever acknowledge that irony in your meetings together?

No, the filmmaking core at Amazon MGM are just trying to make great films with good filmmakers and that have all different types of messages. They want things to be provocative, and they want to encourage artists to speak their mind. So there was never any pushback from the studio about what we were making.

The original draft by Mark Bianculli wasn’t fully what you saw at the end of this film. The content creator aspect was more inspired by me and how I felt these characters would really make a show. It was really a nuts-and-bolts how-to in the script, and I was like, These people have an agenda and would need a personal message. They would need to be more evangelical to bring these followers in.

So I put it through that prism of, What’s the message they are really telling? And they started to tell this message about the inequalities that are happening and the systems that aren’t working for them in an edutainment kind of way. The Wolf is having fun while educating you on his worldview.

We still made a movie with characters that are on both sides, and at the end of the day, I just want the audience to make their own decision of how they want to enact change. I certainly do not want them to rob banks, but they can be proactive in a lot of different ways if they choose to be.

The movie demands those in power to fix the broken system. Do you think it’s even salvageable? Is it broken beyond repair?

That’s a good question, and I don’t have the answer to it. I hope it’s not [broken beyond repair]. But I do think How to Rob a Bank challenges individuals to change the system. It doesn’t necessarily challenge the people in power to change the system. At the end of the movie, our protagonists, if you want to call them that, took on something that was extremely radical. But what they’re asking you to do is be proactive in the ways that you can: help your friend, give back, find a charity to work for. There are other ways to change your community. Go out and vote for what you believe in. You can change the systems. We still live in a democracy.

But that being said, it does feel hard. It’s daunting. There’s a big power [imbalance], and the movie expresses a lot of that frustration. Can it be changed? I hope so. I hope it’s empowering and inspiring to people. Get out there and try to do something about it.

Instead of auditioning, did Nicholas Hoult just send you a copy of his recent movie The Order in which he plays a bankrobber?

(Laughs.) First of all, Nick didn’t have to audition. We’ve been circling projects for years. I think Nick is one of the great actors of his generation, and he’s now coming into his own. He really responded to the contemporary material as much as Kelly [McCormick] and I did. It had something to say, and we knew we could lean into that in a fun way. So I can’t say enough about Nick.

His first day on set, he didn’t really understand how I was going to create this content creator world. He got to set late after we’d already been shooting for a week, and dressed as the Wolf in a security guard outfit, he had to deliver this whole monologue about the security guards’ struggles to make ends meet. And he was like, “Wait, what movie am I in right now?” (Laughs.) But he took it all in stride and really embraced the charismatic nature that this guy had to have to create such a successful YouTube show.

Nick had a tough go of it on this movie. He basically had to shoot it on one leg.

Did the wolf mask come in handy considering he had a torn ACL?

The mask actually helped us in a lot of ways. We did this movie at a lower price point. It was a little smaller budget, and that’s partly because you have to make original content for a price. That’s how the economics of film work.

So we had the heist crew, played by stunt performers, out there shooting the [YouTube robbery] stuff on prosumer cameras, including DJI drones and Insta360s. We did that as second unit with stunt people because they were all in the masks, and we could create a lot of footage for the social media content. I could then really focus on the drama with Pete [Davidson], John [C. Reilly], Zoe [Kravitz], Nick, Anna [Sawai], Rhenzy [Feliz]. That’s the other half of the film, and it’s shot in a very different way. So the masks helped.

When Nick’s character is limping in the street, was that his real limp? Or did he embellish it since the character had been beaten up at that point?

He was leaning into it. He was embellishing it. He was embracing the beating that he took in the garage and pulling his character together. It wasn’t an extension of reality.

Keanu had a bad knee on the first Wick, though not torn-ACL-level bad. It’s actually been a recurring issue on all of them. In any event, you’ve probably got a playbook for this sort of thing, right?

Yeah, I do. There’s a lot of ways to shoot action, and there’s a lot of movie magic that can happen in that space. It’s all about how you choose to choreograph something and how you choose to capture it. Fortunately, Keanu is another person who’s probably the toughest human being on the planet. He just powered through it. We were able to film those sequences with him really doing the action, and the first Wick was 99 percent Keanu.

With Nick and How to Rob a Bank, there’s not as much action, but there is that fight scene in the garage. It was probably his biggest physical set piece, and it was mostly him, barring a crash into a window where someone could get really hurt.

You mentioned that you shot this movie for a price, but you still managed to capture the real-life drama on 35mm film and the Who’s Hungry? social media material on digital. How much arm twisting did you have to do to pull off a dual format?

It was a lot of number crunching, as you always have to do. No matter what size budget, there’s always number crunching, and it usually ultimately comes down to days. We shot this in 40 days, and just to give you context, The Fall Guy was 86 days. So How to Rob a Bank is half the size of that film, and we just had to move quicker. There was a little more planning involved, and we chose a style that required less coverage. So all those things were put through the prism of making a film of this size.

It’s expensive to shoot on film because we generally no longer shoot on film. It’s kind of a bespoke process, so there’s less people doing it, and it’s just more expensive. It’s a bummer because it’s a great format with such a beautiful aesthetic, and it just reacts to light so much differently. I grew up shooting film as a second unit director, and it was right around the time I started directing on the first Wick where digital just basically took over. So it has always been a financial matter, but it was really fun to go back to it.

Early on, Zoe’s character speaks on behalf of her guinea pig named Morpheus. Was she upset that you dubbed over her voice with your own voice?

(Laughs.) She was not upset because she didn’t know about it. During the mix, we were limited in terms of time. We were running out of mix days. So Mark Stoeckinger, who’s a great sound designer that I’ve worked with since Wick, was like, “We need something for the guinea pig. Just get on the mic. Let’s go.” So he put my voice through his beautiful machine, and next thing you know, that’s my cameo.

Zoe is in for a big surprise at the premiere.

The John Wick documentary, Wick is Pain, revealed that the Wick choreography was originally intended for Jason Statham in Safe, but the final product only has a small trace of it.

You are now in post on a movie called Jason Statham Stole My Bike. Is this Jason’s way of saying he regrets not utilizing that style way back when?

(Laughs.) I don’t think it’s his way of saying that. Jason and I have had a longtime friendship. We go way back to my time as a fight choreographer and a stunt performer on Ghosts of Mars. He was the third lead in that film. I did some stunts for him on that, and then we did a lot of choreography together in other films along the way. So we’ve offered up a lot of different styles for him, but he’s made his own brand. It’s been working pretty well for him, so he’s going to be okay.

Is this movie even more meta than The Fall Guy?

It’s its own thing. It’s very different from The Fall Guy. The meta of The Fall Guy was really reflective of the industry, and it was ultimately a romcom surrounded by a meta action film. Jason Statham Stole My Bike is as unique as the title itself, and it is an entertaining ride that’s going to hopefully be a fun four-quadrant film with a lot of twists and turns that people aren’t going to expect.

The last four movies of yours, counting Statham, have been original or semi-original. The Fall Guy and Bullet Train were based on existing works, but they’re first-time adaptations on the big screen. It seems to me like you’re happier in this realm, but are you still open to franchises if they come your way?

I’m open to all of it. I also did a lot of franchises as a second unit director. I spent a lot of time working in a world to amplify a director’s vision or even support studio notes inside of a big franchise. I would shoot that stuff as a second unit director.

But as an artist, I love original material. I love to be allowed to create the world and set the aesthetic — and not have the expectation of what the IP brings to it. It just allows you to have a truer voice of who you are as an artist, so I appreciate you thinking about that.

Original material is harder to get funded, though. It just is. That’s again why we had to do How to Rob a Bank for a smaller price. And Jason Statham Stole My Bike is even smaller in the sense that it’s such a bold idea. But it doesn’t bother me. It’s a problem-opportunity. So, at the end of the day, it’s more fun for me to be original.

***How to Rob a Bank opens in theaters Nov. 13.

#807. Why Joshua Jackson Was Only Dawson's Creek Star Missing From Memoir

In Kerr Smith’s new memoir I Don’t Want to Wait: My Life on Dawson’s Creek, Joshua Jackson was not interviewed like this fellow cast—and Smith shared why in an exclusive E! News interview.

Kerr Smith didn’t want to wait to tell his Dawson’s Creek story.

And so, fans of The WB series might notice that while Katie Holmes, Michelle Williams and James Van Der Beek sat for interviews for his new memoir I Don’t Want to Wait: My Life on Dawson’s Creek, Joshua Jackson did not return to Capeside—and that wasn’t Smith’s decision.

“All I want to say is everybody makes a choice about whether or not they want to be part of the project or not,” Smith told E! News in an exclusive interview. “Some did, some didn't.”

And Smith appeared to nod to Jackson’s hesitation to participate in a parenthetical within the book itself, which hit shelves today, Nov. 10, while recounting that scene between Holmes’ Joey and Jackson’s Pacey in the series finale.

While pushing back on Holmes’ admission that she didn’t love her performance, Smith revealed Jackson wasn’t available to share his perspective.

“Allow me to weigh in with my expert analysis. (Yep, I’m now an expert. I mean, have you not heard? I wrote the book on this stuff.),” Smith wrote. “With all due respect, you’re wrong. You positively crushed this scene. Both of you. Right, Josh? Josh? (I’m sure he’ll get back to me any second now.)”

E! News reached out to Jackson’s rep for comment but hasn’t heard back.

But while Smith and Jackson didn’t go down memory lane, or rather creek, together, the Final Destination alum emphasized what it meant to him to revisit series with the rest of the cast and crew.

“I wanted to get everybody else’s memory on it too,” Smith told E!. “I did over two dozen interviews for the book so I wanted to get everybody’s experiences and put it in one place to understand what a great show this is.”

When it came to his conversations with Holmes, the 54-year-old mused that it was easy for them to simply snap right back into the late 1990s, adding, “It’s like we never even lost a step.”

“You make those bonds back then and you just kind of hang on to them,” he added. “It doesn’t matter how many years have gone by.”

And, of course, it was especially sentimental for Smith to get to reminisce with Van Der Beek before his death earlier this year after a three-year battle with colorectal cancer.

“When I did interview James, he was already pretty sick,” Smith noted. “But he was kind enough to give me a few hours and we had an amazing discussion.”

In addition to being a reflection on Dawson’s Creek as a whole, Smith also included a chapter for former cast and crew to share their memories with Van Der Beek following his death.

“I wanted to give everybody that knew him back then a chance to say anything at all if they wanted to,” Smith shared. “I just thought it was really nice. I think it’s something that he would’ve been OK with.”

As he put it, “I think it’s a good way to end the story.”

You can read the entire fantastic, Steven Spielberg-film worthy story in Smith’s new memoir, and keep reading for even more secrets into the beloved teen drama…

While Fox was first to pick up Dawson's Creek, it subsequently dumped the teen drama.

"I was told they were struggling with Party of Five and they didn't need another one," series creator Kevin Williamson said at the 2015 ATX TV Festival.

But that paved the way for The WB to pick it up two years later.

While Paula Cole's "I Don't Want to Wait" became the iconic Dawson's Creek theme song, producers originally wanted Alanis Morissette's "Hand in My Pocket."

Alas, they couldn't land the rights, what a jagged little pill.

Dawson. Pacey. Joey. Not names you hear every day. So how did Williamson come up with them?

"Dawson came from a real place called Dawson's Creek where we all hung out as kids and partied," he told The Hollywood Reporter in 2018, while Pacey "came from a friend of a friend named Pacey and I'd never met anyone with that name and thought it was a cool name."

And for the show's heroine, Williamson "wanted Josephine as a very girly name that could easily turn into a tomboy name like Joey."

Remember Dawson's infamous "walk the dog" line in the pilot?

Williamson inserted the euphemism because the network would not let them say the word "masturbate" in 1998.

Before Katie Holmes was cast in the role that would make her America's sweetheart-next-door, Blair was this close to landing the role.

"Joe was written to be a tomboy and everyone was coming in being very much a tomboy. We were very close to going with Selma Blair, who was amazing," Williamson told THR. "She read it very tough, with a lot of heart."

However, once he saw Holmes on tape, with "those two big eyes," Williamson knew they had their Joey.

Williamson liked Joshua Jackson so much, he didn't care what role the Mighty Ducks alum played.

"I fell in love with Josh Jackson because he could read any role, Dawson or Pacey," he told THR. "But something wasn't complete and that's when the network said they didn't see Josh as Dawson, and rightfully so. So, I went, 'OK, he's Pacey,' because I knew I wanted him in the show no matter what."

Charlie Hunnam Auditioned, Won Role of Husband

An 18-year-old Charlie Hunnam read for the WB drama in 1999 and, while he didn't land the part, he did meet Katherine Towne at his audition.

They tied the knot in Las Vegas three weeks later and divorced in 2002, "three terrible, painful, expensive years later," as Hunnam put it to the Associated Press in 2017.

Dawson's Creek became so popular that American Eagle inked a deal in 2000 to outfit the actors.

The characters wore mostly AE clothes throughout season three, and the cast appeared in ad campaigns and promos for the clothing line, helping drive the company's net income above $105 million in 2001.

When James Van Der Beek was first cast, the studio wanted him to change his hair.

"We found an ad for The Devil's Own, the movie with Brad Pitt," he recalled to The Daily Beast in 2012. "They said: 'What about Brad Pitt's haircut?' That's how I got my season one haircut."

Holmes dated Jackson early in the show's run, before Pacey and Joey realized they opposite-of-hated each other.

"I'm just going to say that I met somebody last year," Holmes told Rolling Stone in 1998, not denying that the somebody was Jackson. "I fell in love, I had my first love, and it was something so incredible and indescribable that I will treasure it always. And that I feel so fortunate because he's now one of my best friends. It's weird, it's almost like a Dawson-and-Joey type thing now."

Plus one more nugget: "He's been in the business so long," she added, "and he's really helped me. I respect him as a friend and a professional."

When Kerr Smith first signed on to join the show as Joey's new boyfriend, he had no idea the character would eventually come out and be part of the first-ever gay kiss on TV.

"I always knew I wanted Jack to come out of the closet, but I didn't even tell [Smith]," Williamson said at the ATX TV Festival. "Let the audience love him, then let's have him come out of the closet and have Joey have to deal with that—and then that would eventually drive her back to [Dawson]."

More poignantly, Williamson has said that every character on the show inherited traits from him, including Jack.

“Every single character has a trait of me in them,” he told Entertainment Weekly in 2018. “I had just, in my 20s, gone through the coming-out process and had told my parents I was gay. I had taken that whole journey, and I wanted a character on the show to represent that journey and to represent that side of me."

Jack's coming out episode, cowritten by Williamson and producer Greg Berlanti, was inspired by true events.

"A friend of mine had a story that I brought in that he got outed accidentally," Berlanti told EW, "because he wrote a love poem that it was so clear to everyone else that it was about a guy.”

Michelle Williams and Busy Philipps' best-friendship, which first blossomed on Dawson's Creek, is still going strong to this day.

“I’m so in love with her,” Williams told People of her bestie at a 2016 screening of Manchester by the Sea, one of many red carpet date nights for the besties. “She’s proof that the love of your life does not have to be a man! That’s the love of my life right there.”

Philipps is also godmother to Williams' daughter Matilda Ledger, who was born in 2005.

Dawson finally losing his virginity was such a big show moment that Van Der Beek brought a very special gift to set the day the scene was filmed.

"I remember bringing champagne for the crew—Dawson finally lost his virginity!" he told The Daily Beast.

Before starring on One Tree Hill, Chad Michael Murray had an arc on Dawson's Creek playing Charlie, a love interest for Jen and Joey.

But while Charlie got around, Murray didn't seem to make a lot of friends during his first stint in North Carolinav (OTH later filmed there).

During a Paley panel in 2009, Philipps called him "a douche," later saying, "Don't worry. I'm not real worried about burning bridges with CMM."

Van Der Beek added, "He's actually come a long way." Post-event, Philipps tweeted, "Just finished the dawson's creek panel. Maybe I was too harsh on chadM2… Nah."

Murray, meanwhile, hasn't stirred the pot, saying in 2015 that he learned a lot from the experience.

“I had the opportunity to learn from people who had been doing it for a couple of years longer than I was when I walked into the Dawson’s cast,” he told Cosmpolitan.com in 2015. “You know, Michelle and James and Katie and Josh—they really kind of guided me, because they’d already been around for five, six years, maybe longer. And if they had the time, they were showing me the ropes. I had no idea what lighting was, I had no idea about a lot of the technical aspects of what we do, and so I’m grateful for that experience.”

Just a sampling of the famous faces, ranging from the already familiar to future huge stars, who appeared on Dawson's Creek over the years: Seth Rogen, Jane Lynch, Julie Bowen, Scott Foley, Jensen Ackles, Hilarie Burton, Rachel Leigh Cook, Ali Larter and Oliver Hudson.

Young Americans was a short-lived spinoff centering on Pacey's friend Will Krudski (Rodney Scott) and his boarding school classmates at Rawley Academy.

Also starring Ian Somerhalder and Kate Bosworth, it was canceled after just one season.

The Show Almost Ended With Joey Picking Dawson

The show's main love triangle officially disassembled when Joey chose Pacey in the 2003 series finale.

But it almost didn't turn out that way, as Williamson first envisioned Dawson getting the girl. But halfway through writing the finale, Williamson realized that a happy ending for that couple wasn't "what the show was set to be."

"I wanted it to be a twist on the teen genre but also wanted it to be surprising, honest and real and say something about soul mates and what soul mates can be," he explained at the ATX TV Festival. "That's why we did it that way. When you left the show in that last moment, they're a family and everyone got what they wanted. There was fulfillment and they were all happy."

At the last minute, he changed his mind and the rest is TV history. But Williamson admitted his mom, who played for Team Dawson, was not happy.

In the finale, which jumped ahead five years, the group had to deal with the devastating loss of Jen.

"Dealing with the death of one of their own was the final thing that thrust them into adulthood forever. Dawson's Creek was a coming-of-age story and that was the idea behind that ending," Williamson explained of the decision. "That's why we killed Jen, because I wanted them to deal with a death of one their own as that final lesson."

Some of the executive producers who get their start on Dawson's?

Julie Plec (who went on to gift us with The Vampire Diaries and The Originals), Berlanti (Everwood, Arrow, The Flash, Riverdale...the list goes on and on, and that doesn't even include his movies), Rob Thomas (Veronica Mars and iZombie), Jenny Bicks (Sex and the City), Anna Fricke (Being Human), Dana Baratta (Jessica Jones) and many more.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

SpaceX just launched a classified mission for the U.S. military.

A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from California's Vandenberg Space Force Base this evening (Nov. 6) at 7:48 p.m. EST (4:48 p.m. local California time; 0048 GMT on Nov. 7), rising into the sky as the sun sank toward the Pacific.

The launch kicked off the USSF-432 mission for the U.S. Space Force, which we know little about. Neither SpaceX nor the Space Force told us much about USSF-432 beforehand, and we learned tonight; SpaceX cut its webcast off about 10 minutes into the flight, shortly after the Falcon 9's first stage came back to Earth for a landing.

That touchdown occurred aboard the SpaceX droneship "Of Course I Still Love You," which was stationed downrange in the Pacific Ocean. It wrapped up the eighth flight for this particular booster, which is designated 1095.

The Falcon 9's upper stage, meanwhile, continued carrying its mystery payload skyward. It could be headed to low Earth orbit, outside observers speculate.

"It is possibly a batch of classified LEO satellites for the USSF's Space Based Sensing and Targeting (SBST) portfolio based on SpaceX's Starshield satellite bus, based on locations of rocket stage drop zones being exact fits with previous Starlink Group 15 launches," NextSpaceflight.com wrote in a mission description.

Starlink is SpaceX's LEO broadband megaconstellation, which consists of more than 11,000 active satellites. Starshield is a similar system designed to provide services to the U.S. military and its allies. Starshield satellites are believed to be based heavily on the Starlink spacecraft bus.

USSF-432 was the 119th Falcon 9 launch of 2026, and the 14th national-security flight of the rocket so far this year. The vast majority of Falcon 9 missions in 2026 — more than 70% — have been devoted to building out the Starlink megaconstellation.

SpaceX has also launched six other missions this year. Three were operational flights of the company's Falcon Heavy rocket, while the other three were test missions of its next-gen Starship vehicle. SpaceX plans to retire both the Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy shortly after the fully reusable Starship, the biggest and most powerful rocket ever built, is up and running.

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. Gerhard Schenk is a professor and senior research leader at the School of Chemistry and Molecular Biosciences and the Biosustainability Hub, University of Queensland, Brisbane, Australia.

Paul Evans is a research fellow at the School of Chemistry and Molecular Biosciences and the Australian Centre for Ecogenomics, University of Queensland, Brisbane, Australia.

Alan Tordoir is the director of new mining technology at Mining3, Basel, Switzerland.

Susan T. L. Harrison is a professor in bioprocess engineering and deputy vice-chancellor of research and innovation at the University of Queensland, Brisbane, Australia.

Copper compounds (blue) can be extracted from solution using microorganisms — a process known as bioleaching. Credit: Dirk Wiersma/Science Photo Library

The clean-energy transition is creating a paradox. To expand renewable-energy technologies, electrify transport and build infrastructure for artificial intelligence, society must extract unprecedented quantities of minerals. Demand for many of these ‘critical minerals’ is projected to increase several-fold over the coming decades1. Yet, the technologies used to obtain them remain rooted in an old model through which single metals are extracted from virgin ore2.

The consequences are increasingly apparent (see ‘Critical-mineral supply under pressure’). As deposits of high-grade ores decline, larger quantities of rock must be mined and processed to produce the same amount of metal3. That requires more energy and water. Mining accounts for around 1.7% of global energy consumption and this number is projected to rise by up to eight-fold by 20604. Many critical-mineral projects operate in regions facing high water stress, such as arid parts of Africa and Latin America1.

Sources: Top to bottom: Ref. 3; ref. 3; ref. 6 and go.nature.com/4nzbbnx

Mining waste is growing, too. Already, hundreds of billions of tonnes of mine tailings are stored globally. Projections suggest that by 2050, up to two trillion tonnes of extra waste rock and tailings will have accumulated3,5.

Meanwhile, society is producing vast quantities of metal-rich waste that remain a mostly untapped secondary source of metals. In 2022, 62 million tonnes of electronic waste (e-waste) was produced globally — almost 8 kilograms for every person on the planet — and only around 22% of that was formally collected and recycled6.

How to widen access to the critical minerals that the world needs

How to widen access to the critical minerals that the world needs

Many discarded electronics contain valuable metals, including gold, palladium and rare-earth elements — in concentrations that can exceed those found in primary ores. However, recovering these metals remains technically challenging and is often economically unattractive using conventional approaches.

Retrieval of metals and increasing metal circularity should be seen as a strategic capability to offset the growth of metal extraction from virgin ores. Nations that can efficiently recover critical minerals from waste streams, mine residues and low-grade resources will be less exposed to geopolitical disruptions and supply-chain shocks7.

Biology offers a powerful route forwards. Although biomining — which uses microorganisms to extract metals — was once considered a niche approach, it has evolved. Driven by advances in microbial ecology, synthetic biology, structural biology, protein engineering and machine learning, the scientific foundations for a new generation of mineral biotechnologies are emerging at speed8,9. These methods offer potential levels of selectivity for extracting and recovering certain metals that are often difficult to achieve through conventional hydrometallurgical processes.

But, scientific progress alone will not transform mineral supply chains. The main obstacle is no longer a shortage of ideas. It is a lack of pathways from scientific discovery to industrial deployment. Here we outline how to develop those pathways, drawing on discussions at the International Workshop on Biomining of Critical Minerals and Elements, which was sponsored by the Novo Nordisk Foundation and held in Sitges, Spain, in September last year.

Biotechnologies have demonstrated their industrial potential for decades. Bioleaching and biooxidation processes are already established for recovering copper, nickel, gold and cobalt from ores10. They involve irrigating heaps of crushed ore or treating ground mineral powders with specialist microbes that generate chemicals, such as acids or modifiers of reduction–oxidation reactions, that selectively dissolve either target metals or other minerals found with them.

Advances in synthetic biology have expanded the range of potential applications. For example, engineered microbial systems can be designed to dissolve metals more effectively. Biomolecules (such as the protein lanmodulin) can separate rare-earth elements with yields of 99.9% in one step under conditions that are simpler than conventional techniques, using aqueous solutions rather than organic solvents8,11. AI-assisted protein design is further accelerating the discovery of macromolecules designed to selectively recognize, bind to and separate target metals from complex solutions of several elements9.

How the rush for critical minerals is neglecting human needs

How the rush for critical minerals is neglecting human needs

Collectively, these developments suggest that biotechnology could become an important component of future critical-mineral supply chains. However, many promising approaches never progress beyond being validated in the laboratory. They often stall between proof-of-concept studies and commercial demonstration, a challenge familiar throughout industrial biotechnology. Even promising technologies often struggle to attract the capital, infrastructure and industrial partnerships needed to scale them up12,13.

Barriers must be overcome. Although a few bioprocessing pilot projects exist, their capacity is insufficient to evaluate technologies across the diverse types of ore, feedstock and process conditions encountered in practice. Investors are reluctant to finance first-of-a-kind projects when it is uncertain how well they will perform in the real world.

Regulatory frameworks for emerging biomining technologies are also inadequate. They often vary across biotechnology, environmental and mining sectors and between jurisdictions. Developers might need to navigate several regulatory authorities and approval pathways, creating uncertainty and delays as technologies advance.

Electronic waste can contain higher concentrations of key metals than are found in natural ores.Credit: Martin Bernetti/AFP via Getty

In the European Union, for example, the use of genetically modified microorganisms and their environmental applications are subject to distinct regulatory frameworks. Genetically modified microorganisms are allowed to be used in contained systems, whereas those used for field applications generally rely on naturally occurring or adapted microbial strains. The United States uses a coordinated multi-agency approach, involving the Environmental Protection Agency, the Food and Drug Administration and the US Department of Agriculture.

Valuable technical knowledge (on protein engineering, mineral characterization, hydrometallurgy and economic modelling, for instance) remains dispersed across disciplines, institutions and jurisdictions. This makes it difficult to generate the necessary evidence base — including long-term continuous operating data, metrics for tracking chemical cycles and validated economic assessments — to support large-scale adoption of such technologies.

The result is a growing mismatch. Scientific advances in mineral biotechnology are accelerating, yet the mechanisms needed to deploy them are not keeping pace. Although billions of dollars are being invested to secure future supply chains for critical minerals, comparatively little attention has been devoted to building the innovation systems required to commercialize biological solutions.

If biotechnology is to contribute meaningfully to critical-mineral security, environmental sustainability and circularity of resource use, then governments, industry, development banks and philanthropic funders must move beyond supporting research alone. They must invest in the institutions that enable translation of these new technologies as well.

Countries should establish shared pilot and demonstration facilities dedicated to mineral biotechnology. Individual companies often cannot justify the risks associated with developing specialized infrastructure for technologies that remain commercially unproven. Shared facilities can help to overcome this barrier by allowing several organizations to evaluate biological processes using realistic feedstocks under industrially relevant conditions. These facilities can support both pre-commercial and competitive studies. Similar approaches have been implemented successfully in synthetic biology and bio-refining, advanced manufacturing and in the clean-energy and semiconductor sectors.

The dark side of green technology: what do electric vehicles really cost?

The dark side of green technology: what do electric vehicles really cost?

For the mineral sector, such facilities should be located near relevant resource and waste streams, including mining districts, e-waste recycling hubs and sites affected by acid mine drainage or metal-laden urban waste waters. They should have connections to universities, research labs and a skilled workforce.

Access to research and engineering expertise would enable rapid iteration, troubleshooting and integration of mineral biotechnologies with established processes. Such sites would extend beyond technology testing to generate the operational, environmental and economic data needed to inform investment decisions, regulatory approvals and commercial deployment.

Initiatives in other sectors illustrates the value of such infrastructure. In Sweden, for instance, publicly funded pilot and demonstration facilities have been set up to test processes for biochemically converting biomass under realistic conditions14.

#804. Black Lives Matter Activist DeRay Mckesson Talks Losing Key Trump-Era Protest Mobilization Tool: “I Miss Twitter”

The ‘Pod Save the People’ co-host was discussing street-level protests versus policy advocacy with 'The Hollywood Reporter' editor-in-chief Maer Roshan while at Web Summit 2026 in Lisbon, Portugal.

Activist DeRay Mckesson, while today a podcaster and digital storyteller, in 2014 first made a name for himself as a street-level Black Lives Matter protester and a leading voice against police violence.

So Mckesson has a unique perspective as both a social issues activist at the street level and behind a microphone and in front of a camera. And on Tuesday at the Web Summit in Lisbon, he pointed with nostalgia to a once-powerful protest mobilization tool no longer at hand.

“I miss Twitter. Twitter rest in peace. It was such a powerful platform for us back then,” Mckesson, an executive director of Campaign Zero, argued during a session entitled From Chaos to the Campaign moderated by Maer Roshan, editor-in-chief of The Hollywood Reporter and also webcast. Related Stories Business The Hollywood Reporter Launches Turkish Edition General News Trump Reflects on Republicans' Midterm Losses, Reacts to J.D. Vance's Own Analysis in '60 Minutes' Interview

Roshan, who was part of ACT UP, a 1980s group that redefined social activism, and McKesson discussed whether chaotic street protests or strategic policy work were more effective drivers of political change.

In response, McKesson praised the subversive utility of Twitter and Vine to get protesters onto the street. Of course, that’s before Donald Trump was first elected U.S. president, Elon Musk rebranded Twitter as X and slower-paced content from Instagram and TikTok increasingly came to dominate the social media space.

He added Instagram and TikTok had changed digital storytelling by getting civil rights activists away from tweeting in real time for rapid mobilization to taking longer and being more polished with content they distribute across social media platforms. “Especially on Instagram, capturing video footage and getting it out takes time,” Mckesson argued.

At the same time, the recent U.S. midterm elections underlined how civil rights campaigners today use Instagram and TikTok more widely and effectively to talk about candidates and competing stances on hot-button issues. “There are way more people with access to stories and sort of talking because of Instagram and TikTok, in a way that does feel different,” Mckesson insisted.

Elsewhere, he pointed to New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani as a social media master using an influencer operation to get the issue of affordability top-of-mind among New Yorkers when he first ran for political office. And ten years after Trump got to the White House, Mckesson argued social justice content creators enjoy greater traction as Americans increasingly tired of the U.S. president.

“ICE was a big part of the backlash to Trump,” he said of dramatic protests after hooded immigration enforcement agents made arrests at school graduations and birthday parties and attempted deportations across America.

Mckesson said opposition to ICE agent protests more easily cut through and were amplified compared to a decade ago: “In 2014-15, we were a small group of people worried about ICE. Now there’s huge groups of people who don’t even identify as protesters or activists and are pushing on ICE. There are reporters questioning jail deaths in a way that just wasn’t happening.”

And mainstream media is today more likely to cover and raise the alarm on social and political issues and enable calls to grassroots change. “We do see legacy media sort of helping us challenge systems when some of the stuff is just so bizarre, but people think that’s normal,” Mckesson told the Web Summit informal conversation.

Today, he is also co-host of the Pod Save the People podcast from Crooked Media that explores social justice, culture and politics via a platform a long ways from street-level protests during the Black Lives Matter movement. Mckesson insists he’s fine advocating to the converted when it comes to supporting people of color and representing underrepresented voices calling for meaningful change.

“I’m okay with preaching to the choir. The choir needs good messaging. I do think people are smarter today than they were in 2014. People can handle nuanced conversation in a way that is actually really powerful,” he said.

#803. David Walliams Denies Sexual Misconduct Allegations

British comedian David Walliams responded to allegations of sexual misconduct published by The Guardian and ITV, denying claims against him: "I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law."

After The Guardian and ITV published a wide-ranging exposé accusing the former Britain's Got Talent judge of sexual misconduct, including sexual harassment, grooming and abusing his power to sexually prey on women and teenagers as young as 15, he broke his silence to vehemently deny the allegations.

"Looking back, I realize that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with," Walliams, 55, said in a Nov. 10 statement to the outlets, which joined forces for a three-year joint investigation into the accusations made against him. "I realize I did not always take people's feelings properly into account. That is something I regret."

"Whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did," the comedian continued. "I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me." (The age of consent in the U.K. is 16.)

The article was published earlier on Nov. 10, days after a judge rejected Walliams's injunction to prevent its publication. (Walliams, whose attorney said in court he had attempted suicide twice in the months leading up to the publication, per The Guardian, was seeking psychiatric treatment.) Multiple women—who were identified with pseudonyms after agreeing to speak with the publications under the condition of anonymity—accused Walliams of being "predatory" and "pushy" during the alleged interactions beginning in 2003.

Two of his accusers alleged that they met the children's book author when they were minors, including a woman identified as Alex, who said she was 15 when she met him at an autograph signing in 2004 where she gave him her cover letter in hopes of exploring a comedy writing career, according to The Guardian.

Alex alleged that she and Walliams exchanged multiple emails—which were included in the publication—and occasionally spoke on the phone for two years. She said that he suggested that he could help her succeed in the comedy world.

By 17, she said that they were having sex. "I think I was groomed, 100 percent," she told The Guardian. "We met when I was 15 and he was promising to help me and was a figure of authority and someone that I looked to for guidance and help."

Another woman, referred to as Jade, also alleged she was 15 when she had met Walliams. She said that after the then-36-year-old reached out to her on MySpace in 2007—which Jade said clearly showed her date of birth—he invited her to his home, where he kissed her.

Other accounts—ITV and The Guardian cited speaking with 30 sources with first-hand knowledge of his behavior—were from women between 18 and early 20s who alleged Walliams tried to use his fame and wealth to coerce them into sex.

One such accuser, Sarah, 18, alleged that Walliams took an interest in her after meeting him during filming for Britain's Got Talent, according to The Guardian. He eventually invited the starstruck teen to his London home, with her alleging that he attempted to have sex with her while she was drunk and unable to walk properly, but her friend intervened. She said she and her friend ultimately slept in a spare bedroom.

Walliams' attorney emphasized that his client denied any wrongdoing with all of the women, also refuting Sarah's allegation that he got her "drunk to take advantage of her."

E! News has reached out to Walliams' reps and HarperCollins UK for comment and has not yet heard back.

Unspecified allegations were previously made against Walliams—who shares a son with ex Lara Stone—by at least five female employees at his publisher HarperCollins in December 2025, per The Guardian.

The company ultimately dropped him, telling The Telegraph at the time, "After careful consideration, and under the leadership of its new CEO, HarperCollins UK has decided not to publish any new titles by David Walliams."

Walliams's agent told the outlet in a statement that his client "strongly denies that he has behaved inappropriately."

"I think the implications are pretty severe, which is why we're taking it so seriously and putting such extreme focus on the mission right now."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman is serious about launching "big rockets" to the moon every single year for the agency's Artemis program. And the new space race with China is fueling that ambition.

"I feel good. I feel like we are certainly on a more achievable path to the lunar surface today than where we were before," Isaacman told Space.com.

We recently sat down with the NASA chief to discuss the state of the Artemis program, and, off the bat, he made it clear that he's confident in the U.S. space program following the success of April's Artemis II mission around the moon. In fact, just prior to our conversation, it was announced that Artemis II commander Reid Wiseman will become the new deputy director of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory. But the road from Artemis II's success to crewed lunar landings and, later, a permanent moon base will take a lot of launches of NASA's Space Launch System (SLS) megarocket, Isaacman stressed.

"You know, a lot of people, especially in the space community, start getting [into] if the landers are there or not. I don't really care about that right now. What I care about is that we are launching big rockets no less than once a year," he said.

"I think that's imperative for NASA to be doing these deep-space human spaceflight missions right now," Isaacman added. "So, we had a great mission in April of '26. We will launch again in '27."

That coming launch will be for Artemis III, a crewed mission to low Earth orbit that will test docking procedures between NASA's Orion capsule and one or both of the Artemis program's private lunar landers — SpaceX's Starship and Blue Origin's Blue Moon.

"We need to continue to exercise those muscles," he said, referring to SLS liftoffs. "And, honestly, once a year isn't great, either. I mean, I don't think we're going to get back to the early [space] shuttle days, you know, four missions a year. I don't think we're going to get back to where we were with Apollo, but once a year is the minimum … I would testify that to Congress in this role years down the road.

"If NASA is going to be doing deep-space missions, complicated missions, [we should] launch at least once a year and get as much out of it as you can for taking the risk and spending the taxpayer dollars and building towards something greater," Isaacman added. "That's what we're doing with Artemis III, and that's what's going to better prepare us for Artemis IV."

So, how is NASA coping with the challenges that face them as they approach Artemis III ahead of a crewed lunar landing on Artemis IV, which is targeted for 2028? While NASA can learn some lessons from past moon missions with Apollo, today it's primarily relying on the extensive experience and talent within the agency, according to Isaacman.

"Artemis II is very different from Apollo 8, and Artemis III will be very different from Apollo 9," he said. "Our approach is not exactly the same as it was … But what is the same right now? The spirit, the energy, the potential within NASA. The talent of the workforce and industry is no different than the 1960s."

There's another similarity to the Apollo era: NASA has a rival in its race to the moon. While the adversary in the 1960s was the Soviet Union, today the U.S. is competing against China.

"It is a real space race," Isaacman said. But, he added, "this one is very different than the first one."

"Everything is closer than it was, not just in space. I mean, we had the edge in computing [and] every one of the technology domains during the Cold War. Our capabilities were better by a mile," he said. "[But with] China, it's not [like that]. They're very close."

"We're saying we're going to land on the moon at the end of 2028. China is saying by the end of 2029," Isaacman added. "And it's like, Well, are they going to pull it off? Yes, they will. They've showcased their landers, their rovers, their suits, two-launch architecture with built-in reusability."

So NASA is taking the Chinese threat very seriously, according to Isaacman.

"The consequence of getting this wrong, I'm telling you — it's going to be felt around the world," he said. "It will call everything into question."

"Should I be using American superintelligence or AI? Should I be doing Chinese? Should I be buying their computers? Should I be [buying] ours? Buying their cars, their airplanes, their ships? Whose security guarantees to trust?" Isaacman added. "I think the implications are pretty severe, which is why we're taking it so seriously and putting such extreme focus on the mission right now. But we have that playbook of success, and I think we will prevail."

Chelsea Gohd served as a Senior Writer for Space.com from 2018 to 2022 before returning in 2026, covering everything from climate change to planetary science and human spaceflight in both articles and on-camera in videos. #801. How Hip-Hop Changed the Billboard Charts: From ‘Rapper’s Delight’ to Today | Billboard News

From Sugarhill Gang’s “Rapper’s Delight” breaking into the Hot 100 to chart milestones from Ms. Lauryn Hill, Eminem, Outkast, Drake and Kendrick Lamar, look back at the moments that helped hip-hop reshape music and culture.

From block parties in the Bronx to the top of the Billboard charts, hip-hop has spent decades breaking records, crossing boundaries, and changing the sound of popular music. In celebration of National Hip-Hop History Month, we’re looking back at the groundbreaking moments that shaped the genre’s rise, the artists who rewrote the record books, and the milestones that changed music forever. This is Billboard News, presented by Lexus. Let’s rewind to 1980, when the Sugarhill Gang’s “Rapper’s Delight” became the first hip-hop single to break into the top 40 of the Billboard Hot 100, reaching No. 36. By 1986, Run-D.M.C. was breaking barriers with Aerosmith on “Walk This Way,” bringing hip-hop to an even wider audience. And in 1989, Billboard launched its first dedicated rap chart, giving the growing genre a new platform to measure its success. By the ’90s, hip-hop wasn’t just climbing the charts, it was taking over. In 1998, Lauryn Hill made history when The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200, setting a new first-week sales record for a female artist at the time. Just a few years later, Eminem’s The Marshall Mathers LP delivered one of the biggest debut weeks in hip-hop history, while Outkast’s “Hey Ya!” spent nine weeks at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100.

#800. ‘Confession’ Review: Rob Lowe and James Franco in a Ben Shapiro-Scripted, Stalinist Russia-Set Drama That’s Terminally Tedious

Jennifer Jason Leigh, Nick Nolte, Emile Hirsch and Kodi Smit-McPhee also appear in Václav Marhoul's film about the brutal interrogation of a prisoner in a Stalin-era Russian jail.

Reviewing the new movie scripted by Ben Shapiro, I’m tempted to pan it on ideological grounds. The screenwriter, after all, is the controversial right-wing political commentator who co-founded The Daily Wire and was editor-at-large at Breitbart News for several years. To say that the vast majority of his views are loathsome to me is an understatement.

Fortunately, it’s easy to write about the film directed by Václav Marhoul without being tainted by political bias. Depicting the brutal interrogation of a prisoner in a Stalin-era Russian jail, Confession proves a dull, turgid slog. The film will be given a one-night theatrical release on November 11, the same day it will be made available on The Daily Wire’s streaming service. Related Stories Midterms 2026 Ben Shapiro Says 2026 Midterms Were "A Wipeout for Republicans": "The President Was Kind of on the Ballot" Movies Oops! How Danny Trejo Accidentally Made a Pro-ICE Movie Confession The Bottom Line Torture, onscreen and off. Release date: Wednesday, November 11Cast: Rob Lowe, James Franco, Jennifer Jason Leigh, Kodi Smit-McPhee, Nick Nolte, Richard Brake, Emile Hirsch, Brad Dourif, Dean NorrisDirector: Václav MarhoulScreenwriter: Ben Shapiro 2 hours 12 minutes

Other than its hardly controversial stance that Stalinist Russia was a very, very bad place, there’s nothing inherently political about the film. Except possibly for the casting of James Franco in a major role, which, like the presence of Jonathan Majors in the company’s recent Run Hide Fight: Infidels, seems designed to give a middle finger to the Hollywood studios for shunning them. In this case, Franco has plenty of distinguished company, with the ensemble including Rob Lowe, Jennifer Jason Leigh, Nick Nolte, Emile Hirsch, Brad Dourif, Dean Norris, and Kodi Smit-McPhee. The story behind that casting would likely prove more interesting than the film itself.

Lowe plays the central role of Alexei, a former literature professor who is arrested in 1938 Moscow, brought to Lubyanka Prison and charged with being a counterrevolutionary. In the sort of coincidence beloved by unimaginative screenwriters, his interrogator is Vladimir (Franco), his former prize student. Vladimir presses his prisoner to inform on Father Mikulski (Dourif), a dissident Eastern Orthodox priest who has published an anti-Soviet pamphlet.

True to the participants’ former roles, the encounter becomes less an interrogation than a literary salon in which the names of Dostoevsky, Pushkin and Tolstoy are dropped so often that a drinking game could be devised from it. The endless verbiage (the film runs a numbing 132 minutes) proves stultifying despite the efforts of the two actors, who give it their all but never manage to be remotely convincing in their roles.

The film essentially takes place in two settings: the interrogation room and the prison cell that Alexei shares with three others, making the claustrophobic proceedings feel very stagebound. Nolte plays a Jewish inmate, giving him the opportunity to deliver a harrowing monologue about atrocities he’s witnessed, which might have been powerful if the actor’s diminished gravelly voice didn’t reduce its impact. Hirsch plays a former concert pianist with an unnaturally cheerful attitude. Richard Brake (Barbarian), giving the film’s most effective performance, plays a hardened, cynical prisoner who coaches Alexei on how to survive.

Alexei’s bitter ex-wife (Leigh) visits him in his cell, exhorting him to inform on the priest. “Damn you and your literary references,” she shouts at Alexie when he resists in typically erudite terms, serving as a de facto proxy for viewers. Also showing up is his estranged son (an unrecognizable Smit-McPhee), angry with his father over the way his mother has been treated.

Then it’s back to the interrogation room, where Vladimir gets much rougher with Alexie, brutally beating him to force him to sign a confession. But his exertions don’t prevent him from having the energy to deliver such ham-fisted lines as “Evil and good are luxuries the revolution can no longer afford.”

Director Marhoul, whose controversial 2019 film The Painted Bird prompted numerous walkouts at the Toronto and Venice film festivals, infuses the film with a suitably gritty, intense tone, abetted by cinematographer Peter Menzies Jr.’s (Shooter, Gods of Egypt) strikingly harsh visuals.

Hopelessly stilted in its execution (it’s the kind of prison drama in which the guards and soldiers speak with all the realism of automatons), the terminally tedious Confession seems mainly designed to demonstrate that its screenwriter benefited from a really good education during which he studied all the Russian literary masters.

The movies might be struggling to recapture the magic, but Star Wars video games are strong with the Force.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

After a tumultuous start to EA's rebooted Star Wars Battlefront series, in 2021 Lucasfilm and Disney decided to open up the development of new Star Wars games by bringing in different publishers and studios under the Lucasfilm Games banner. Now, over five years on, we can confidently say we're entering a new golden era of amazing Star Wars games.

With LucasArts' successor calling the shots and coordinating a multitude of projects set in a galaxy far, far away, even EA's latest efforts like Squadrons and the Jedi series have taken bigger and bolder swings. Now, in 2026, the full potential of the Star Wars universe has become clearer with specific releases squarely aimed at niche audiences.

It's become clear that future Star Wars games needn't be expensive endeavors full of familiar faces or concepts. Star Wars Zero Company and Galactic Racer's restrained scope and confidence have been infectious, and, as it turns out, they're already recognized by all the parties involved as double-A success stories.

A Burnout-inspired Star Wars racer (created by a bunch of ex-Burnout devs) is a fantastic pitch if you know your video games, but looking at EA's recent and current direction, it's easy to see why it didn't happen under their reign. The original Burnout studio, Criterion, would have been an excellent candidate, but instead they were sent to work in the Battlefield mines. Still, someone was interested in the idea, and the end result is glorious.

Fast and furious, Star Wars: Galactic Racer ignores recent racing game trends and bets big on arcade-y vibes, uncomplicated controls, and a high skill ceiling that challenges you with extremely high speeds, tight turns, and unexpected interruptions as other drivers try to ruin your day.

The not-so-secret sauce, however, was its runs-based structure, which injects the flexibility and replay value of roguelite games into the more traditional arcade racing structure that older gamers are familiar with.

Fully confident in its central gameplay idea and devoid of modern live-service baggage, Fuse Games' debut title makes the most of the Star Wars setting within the restrictions of simply making a fun and engaging Star Wars racer.

It's almost the same approach we felt in Zero Company, a turn-based tactical strategy-RPG that comes from the minds of another team of ex-triple-A developers. "Star Wars but XCOM" should've happened earlier, but we're glad it did this year, and, unsurprisingly, it's a banger.

The correct read of their success should be obvious (and so far, it appears the powers that be are seeing it): Let seasoned and fresh developers cook games they're excited about.

Big, medium, or small, players will react positively to experiences that really feel genuine and aren't brought down by tacked-on systems or monetization. Ubisoft's Massive Entertainment also got it right with Star Wars Outlaws, but that ambitious open-world title — hardly a fresh pitch nowadays — also faced high sales expectations due to an inevitably gigantic production budget.

Allowing Star Wars to get weirder and more specific could also help the movie and TV side of things. We know Star Wars has finally locked in clearer big-screen plans for the coming years, and with Disney Plus TV series being seemingly scaled down and targeting more distinct stories better suited for a non-theatrical medium, the crowds' responses to Lucasfilm Games' wins shouldn't be overlooked.

You can't manufacture a viral character like Biddy Blas, arguably Star Wars' most popular new character since Grogu's debut in 2019. It just happens. And it happens naturally if Star Wars is allowed to explore the weird corners of a galaxy.

Devoid of ties to the larger canon and set away from the Imperial era, Galactic Racer makes the post-war period richer by going smaller. It's a reminder of much of the promise introduced by The Mandalorian's first season, before it became distractingly "relevant" to the larger saga.

Even the Clone Wars-set Zero Company keeps things relatively low-profile. Yes, major characters like Anakin Skywalker make cameos, but they don't rob the A-Team and Suicide Squad-inspired tale of camaraderie and subterfuge of its valuable independence. Sure, hits like Andor and Rogue One were obvious inspirations for its tone, but the story stands alone, allowing even Star Wars newcomers to jump in and enjoy it with minimal context.

At a time when giant decades-old franchises often struggle to recruit new fans, the last two Star Wars games reinforce the property's new direction in a medium that can reach more potential Padawans than any other.

The good trick? Just allowing Star Wars to be fresh and smaller — and with no homework required — from time to time. In turn, the larger stories on the horizon will be stronger with the Force.

Command an elite squad in a gritty, authentic Star Wars story set in the twilight of the Clone Wars. Step into the boots of Hawks, a former Republic officer leading Zero Company on a covert operation against an emerging threat that could consume the galaxy.

Available on PS5, Xbox Series X|S, and PC.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer is a ​high-stakes reinvention of racing born in the lawless Outer Rim of the ​​Star Wars galaxy.​​​​

#798. Is Halloween About To Become the New Christmas on the Hot 100?

This week's Five Burning Questions looks at new Oct. 31-boosted chart peaks for Michael Jackson's "Thriller" and Tame Impala & JENNIE's "Dracula."

On this week’s Billboard Hot 100 (dated Nov. 14), Halloween comes closer than ever to boosting a spooky-season anthem to the top of its rankings.

Though Ella Langley’s “Choosin’ Texas” reigns for a 27th week on the listing, a pair of fright-night favorites — one classic and one new — appear right below it, in Michael Jackson‘s “Thriller” and Tame Impala and JENNIE‘s “Dracula,” respectively. Both hit new peaks this week, and lead the six total Halloween-themed titles on this week’s chart, including one first-time entry: “Spooky, Scary Skeletons,” from late ’70s hitmaker Andrew Gold.

Will “Thriller” get to No. 1 one of these years? And will Halloween someday have close to the same annual impact on the Hot 100 as Christmas does? Billboard staffers answer these questions and more below.

Katie Atkinson: It sure looks like it! And the chart tracking week will allow for even more Halloween music action in the coming years, because Halloween was on a Saturday this year, meaning the only Halloweekend activity was Friday through early Sunday. Next year, it falls on a Sunday, allowing for an extra tracking day, and it just goes up from there. With music streaming at an all-time high, the more closely we can follow people’s listening habits, the more these seasonal spikes will occur.

Kyle Denis: I think we just might be! Obviously, not every Halloween will coincide with a $1 billion-grossing Michael Jackson biopic and a hit single that just so happens to share a name with one of the holiday’s most enduring characters, but 2026 certainly helped refine the sub-genre of “Halloween pop.”

Chris Eggertsen: I hope so! Halloween is my favorite holiday, and I’d love to see an influx of songs about ghosts and monsters flood the Hot 100 starting every late September or so. While it does seem we’re moving in that direction, I don’t think it’ll ever quite match the power of Christmas — a holiday in which seasonal music is so deeply embedded — in terms of Billboard chart dominance.

Lyndsey Havens: I think so and I hope so. Halloween may not be as cheery as Christmas, but it is a bit more inclusive and playfully spooky — and that’s something worth getting behind.Andrew Unterberger: I don’t know if we’re ever going to quite get to the regular 40-of-the-top-50 levels of domination Christmas can now claim at its yearly Hot 100 peak — there are still only a half-dozen Halloween-themed titles on this week’s chart, after all. But yes, failing some major shift in listener trends (or how Billboard measures them), it should become more and more of a factor year over year, as the streaming sea level among contemporary hits continues to lower and seasonal perennials continue to stick out like they do.

Katie Atkinson: Yes, “Thriller” is the obvious contender for the perennial Mariah slot. That being said, I think it’s worth remembering that in addition to Halloween, the MJ catalog has been seeing a boost all year thanks to April’s Michael biopic. So I do wonder if that increased popularity factored into the song reaching its No. 2 peak this year. I love seeing Christmas songs climb up the chart every year, and this will be a new fun holiday race to watch — and could even lead to a song like “Thriller” that many people might assume was already a Hot 100 No. 1 hit possibly taking a four-decade-plus route to getting there.

Kyle Denis: I’m going with yes. Chart watchers will remember that “All I Want for Christmas Is You” didn’t hit No. 1 during its first few holiday-induced reentries. Between “Thriller” playing in a far less crowded field in terms of yearly Halloween-themed releases and a new generation of listeners who are freshly enamored with the King of Pop, I can definitely see the song becoming an every-year No. 1, barring a gargantuan competitor like “Choosin’ Texas.”

Chris Eggertsen: Given its fairly steady upward trajectory over the last close to a decade — from lingering just within or just outside the top 40 starting at the end of the 2010s before hitting No. 2 this year —  it certainly does feel like “Thriller” is destined to hit No. 1, though I do wonder how much of the bump this year was due to the release of the smash-hit Michael biopic. Then again, with a Michael sequel in development and MJ’s music seemingly hotter than it’s been in decades, a No. 1 placement is certainly plausible over the next couple of years. I don’t think we’re necessarily looking at a perennial Halloween No. 1 a la “All I Want for Christmas Is You,” though, as “Thriller” doesn’t (yet) feel quite as undeniable as the Mariah classic, which effectively occupies its own airspace in the canon of Christmas songs.

Lyndsey Havens: It sure could. Obviously, this year, the film Michael helped the superstar enjoy sustained bumps across his catalog. So, I do think “Thriller” had a leg up compared to years prior, but that’s not to say it won’t continue for years to come. All it may need to jump to that top spot next year is a thoughtfully strategic campaign to say “it’s tiiiiime” a la Mariah.

Andrew Unterberger: Yeah, it seems inevitable — maybe even next year, when Halloween falls on a Sunday, meaning “Thriller” should get pretty major streaming numbers throughout that entire weekend. But if not next year then someday. Maybe for the 20th anniversary of MJ’s death in 2029, or the Thriller album’s 50th anniversary in 2032.

Katie Atkinson: This one is trickier. (Trick-or-treatier?) I could see it getting an annual bump, but I think No. 3 will be the highest it climbs on the Hot 100. Think of it as the new “Disturbia” or “The Dead Dance” or “Heads Will Roll” — the kind of modern song that is seasonally appropriate and gets playlisted on all the Halloween party soundtracks, but not to a “Thriller” level.

Kyle Denis: I think it remains in the canon, albeit on the more contemporary side, with cuts like Lady Gaga’s “The Dead Dance”; if Kevin Parker’s goal was to deliver the new-school Halloween anthem, he timed the whole thing pretty perfectly! I’ll admit, I’d be a bit surprised not to see “Dracula” post substantial streaming gains next Halloween.

Chris Eggertsen: “Dracula” is only a year old at this point, so it’s a little too early to tell. Can a song that’s only tangentially “spooky” sink its teeth into the Hot 100 every year in the way more straightforward scary-season tracks like “Thriller,” “Monster Mash” and “Ghostbusters” have managed? I’m not convinced of that yet, but a No. 3 placement also can’t be discounted.

Lyndsey Havens: I think it will have to prove itself. As much as I love the song, it’s been a bit of a sleeper hit since JENNIE hopped on the remix in February, which is to say, the song was already becoming a slow but lasting hit well before Halloween. I think the holiday gave it that final boost, of course, but I’m not sure if it’s a repeatable process or timeline for years to come.

Andrew Unterberger: I think it’ll hang around, but it’ll have some work to do before it can really compete with the Halloween heavy-hitters. Even at its new daily streaming peak on Oct. 31, it was still multiple millions behind any of the other spooky songs on the Hot 100 this week — and may be even further back next year as it fades as a contemporary hit. But with this early moment under its belt, cementing it as a Halloween staple so early in its lifespan, it’s in the best position to eventually join the all-time canon of any song of the last decade or two.

Katie Atkinson: As a parent to children under 10, welcome to the “Spooky, Scary Skeletons” party, everyone else! I’ve been a proud annual listener for the better part of a decade, and I think this is a delightful addition to the Halloween Hot 100 hits. The long and winding path of this song is fascinating, too, between Gold releasing it in the ’90s and then it getting an EDM remix that brought it new life in 2013. Add to that the lore of Gold’s previous career as an easy-listening hitmaker AND that he wrote the flipping Golden Girls theme song and this man had one of the most unpredictable career paths of all time. (Sadly, Gold passed in 2011, so he never saw his song’s EDM-fueled online resurgence.)

Kyle Denis: Honestly, the remixed version of “Spooky, Scary Skeletons” goes off during a daytime Halloween party, so I won’t scoff at it being added to the canon.

Chris Eggertsen: On the one hand, I appreciate the over-the-top Halloween energy Gold brings to “Spooky, Scary Skeletons,” which also weirdly feels engineered for TikTok virality even though it was released in 1996. But unlike “Thriller” or “Monster Mash,” it’s not exactly a bop — IMO, the vibe is more “pre-trick or treat vibe-setter for the kiddos” than “all-ages Halloween party standard.” I won’t be mad if it becomes an annual entry on the Hot 100, but personally, I can take it or leave it.

Lyndsey Havens: Yes! I think (almost) every Halloween song ever made is a worthy addition to the Halloween canon, and surely this one is. It’s perfectly aged and fun and boasts an alliterative title, what more could you want? As we’ve seen with non-holiday hits, the power of TikTok cannot be ignored when it comes to reviving music and trends from an early or even pre-social media era, so I think it’s expected and fun that a Halloween song would benefit from that, too.

Andrew Unterberger: “Skeletons” has clearly hooked the next generation, so it seems like it should only become more of a Halloween fixture from here. Now we just have to figure out additional holidays to attach “Lonely Boy” and “Thank You for Being a Friend” to.

Katie Atkinson: I’m so glad you asked this question so I can write about my favorite offbeat Halloween song of all time! Please do yourselves a favor and listen to “Halloween Spooks” by jazz trio Lambert, Hendricks & Ross. It was a running gag on KROQ’s The Kevin & Bean Show here in Los Angeles (RIP) that Bean would play this song every spooky season just to annoy Kevin, but while it was a joke on the show, I legitimately love it. And now I’m playing it every year around the house to annoy my kids instead.

Kyle Denis: It’s a six-minute, two-part song that’s not really radio-friendly at all, but Beyoncé’s “Haunted” is one of my favorite creepy, spooky, Halloween-adjacent pop joints from the past 15 years.

Chris Eggertsen: I hold a special place in my dark heart for Blue Oyster Cult’s “(Don’t Fear) The Reaper,” which is featured in John Carpenter’s original Halloween — the best Halloween movie of all time and one of my personal favorite films ever. In my mind, the song and the film are inextricably linked, and no other track puts me in the Halloween spirit more than that one. Taken on its own merits, it’s a haunting piece of work about accepting your own mortality that gives me literal chills every time I hear it — and I can’t think of a better tribute to its eerie power (side note: it was also, of course, the basis of a classic SNL sketch). It was a top 15 Hot 100 hit when it first came out back in 1976, but it’s become a little overlooked in recent years and I’d love to see it be re-embraced as a seasonal classic.

Lyndsey Havens: I mean, Phoebe Bridgers literally has a song called “Halloween” so that sort of feels like what are we even doing if not bumping that during its namesake holiday? Sure, it’s a bit downtempo and emotive, but you could argue nothing is spookier than being honest about your feelings. She has my vote.

Andrew Unterberger: Ministry’s “Everyday Is Halloween” isn’t about Halloween necessarily — more of an anthem for those sick of being picked on for dressing differently — but there’s still not a song that feels more like Oct. 31 to me; it’s always the first cut I put on before going out for the evening.
