#797. Pacific Palisades’ Bay Theater to Reopen on Friday With Johnny Depp Comeback ‘Ebenezer’

Skydance CEO David Ellison has championed the location as a symbol of his commitment to the community and theatrical exhibition.

Set your calendars: The Bay Theater, the long-shuttered legacy cinema at Palisades Village, is reopening on Friday.

The resurrection marks nearly two years after the 2025 wildfires ravaged the area. Alongside developer Rick Caruso, Skydance CEO David Ellison has championed the venue as something like a town square and a physical symbol of his commitment to theatrical exhibition (RIP the Paramount Decrees).

The theater is reopening just in time for the release of Paramount’s Ebenezer, the studio’s buzzy bet on Johnny Depp’s A-list rehabilitation positioning the actor for a potential Hollywood comeback. The cinema won’t just be showing Skydance titles either. Godzilla Minus Zero, You Can See Everything, Wild Horse Nine and The Cat in the Hat (Warner Bros. Pictures Animation) will also be playing over the weekend.

Paramount Pictures revealed the revival last month, announcing plans to bring first-run theatrical releases, classics and experiential events to the cinema. The location is operated by The Lot, a luxury dine-in theater chain. Ellison has called it a “place for the Pacific Palisades community to gather around the shared experience of cinema,” saying that the Bay is “woven into the fabric of this neighborhood.”

Don’t be surprised if the studio plans to make the Bay its central hub for screenings given Ellison’s proximity to the location.

Caruso has discussed how he envisioned Palisades Village as a more intimate space than his other megapopular properties, The Grove in Los Angeles or the Americana at Brand in Glendale. After the original Bay Theatre closed in 1978, the Pacific Palisades went roughly 40 years without a movie theater of its own, until Caruso revived the name as part of Palisades Village in 2018.

Each theater offers luxury seating — with adjustable foot, back and head rests — USB charging, personal dining tables with custom lighting and service buttons for in-seat ordering. The lobby features a full-service bar with a video wall.

The reopening is part of a broader revival of L.A.’s cinema scene amid this year’s blazing box office run. It includes Sony’s planned restoration of the Cinerama Dome and rehabilitation of the adjacent ArcLight Hollywood, Amazon’s lease of the Culver Theater and Netflix’s purchase of the Egyptian in Hollywood. The resurgence isn’t limited to blockbuster venues either. There’s the Jason Reitman-led return of the Village in Westwood, Quentin Tarantino’s takeover of the Vista in Los Feliz and Kristen Stewart’s resuscitations of the Highland Theatre.

NASA is asking the public to send their names to Titan for an ambitious mission that will see a flying craft explore the Saturn moon in 2034, if all goes according to plan.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

We still may be some time away from sending humans to distant reaches of the solar system, but you can send your name to Saturn's moon Titan, which has the ingredients of life on its surface thanks to NASA's Dragonfly mission.

Dragonfly is an SUV-sized nuclear-powered rotorcraft that NASA aims to launch towards Titan in 2028. The agency opened a special events page in late October to allow members of the public to put their name on the spacecraft. The names will be put upon a chip on Dragonfly during the spacecraft's assembly, and all names must be submitted before Jan. 15, 2027.

The agency says that the mission has no "ordinary itinerary," as Dragonfly aims to between areas miles (or kilometers) apart after arriving on the surface in 2034. "Nearly a billion miles away, an extraordinary destination awaits. Titan has an atmosphere, rivers and lakes, seasons, sweeping dunes and a landscape rich in organic material," NASA officials wrote in the event page. "Upon arrival in 2034, Dragonfly will fly from place to place on this intriguing world to uncover clues about this remarkable moon, and the chemistry that could help us understand the ingredients for life."

Dragonfly will be one of just a few flying crafts on another world, with the first being NASA's plucky Ingenuity mini-helicopter that arrived on Mars along with the still-running Perseverance rover in 2021. Ingenuity was only designed to make five flights, but made it to 72 until its blades were damaged during a landing on Jan. 18, 2024.

NASA is now planning a SkyFall mission on Mars that would use three helicopters, and which may launch as soon as late 2028 for the Red Planet.

Dragonfly, however, is not the first mission to Titan: that would be Huygens, which operated for just a few hours on Jan. 14, 2005 after deploying from the Cassini spacecraft. Huygens was the first lander on an outer solar system world, and measured Titan's atmosphere and took data from the surface.

For its part, Cassini flew by Titan more than 100 times before the mission concluded in September 2017, providing valuable long-term data about the moon from above. Dragonfly aims to show the moon from up close for about 3.3 Earth years. Its destinations will include dunes and a young impact crater called Selk, according to NASA.

"Dragonfly is expected to make one flight every one to two Titan days, which is called a Tsol and lasts about 16 Earth days," NASA officials added of the mission. Dragonfly will stop at a variety of geologic sites, where it will collect samples of surface material for analysis inside the rotorcraft by a suite of scientific instruments."

Dragonfly's goals include learning more about prebiotic chemistry, or the conditions prior to life arising in a location; figuring out if Titan had habitable conditions in the past; and looking for "chemical indicators" of life based on water or hydrocarbons.

Elizabeth Howell (she/her), Ph.D., was a staff writer in the spaceflight channel between 2022 and 2024 specializing in Canadian space news. She was contributing writer for Space.com for 10 years from 2012 to 2024. Elizabeth's reporting includes multiple exclusives with the White House, leading world coverage about a lost-and-found space tomato on the International Space Station, witnessing five human spaceflight launches on two continents, flying parabolic, working inside a spacesuit, and participating in a simulated Mars mission. Her latest book, "Why Am I Taller?" (ECW Press, 2022) is co-written with astronaut Dave Williams.

#795. Broadway Box Office: ‘Much Ado About Nothing’ Hits $2.3 Million As Industry Rebounds

'Here There Are Blueberries' and 'It's A Wonderful Life' began previews, as industry grosses rose 24 percent.

Much Ado About Nothing, starring Tom Hiddleston and Hayley Atwell, shot up to $2.3 million in its first week of eight performances, making it the third highest grossing show of the week, and suggesting it will be a top earner going forward. Capacity was at 100 percent for the show, which is set to open Nov. 19.

The average ticket price for Much Ado About Nothing fell back down to $194, still putting it in the upper echelon, but several rungs below the $315 average ticket price at Other Desert Cities.

Hamilton was the highest grossing show, with $2.7 million, followed by the starry Other Desert Cities, with Julia Louis-Dreyfus, Allison Janney and Joe Keery, with $2.5 million, Much Ado About Nothing, The Lion King with $1.8 million and Harry Potter and the Cursed Child with $1.7 million.

Billy Crystal’s one-man show, 860, remains a top-earner and is rising in gross, with $1.5 million brought in last week. A Few Good Men also remains in the top tier, with $1.44 million last week, despite mixed reviews, as does the Bowen Yang-led Oh, Mary! with $1.4 million. The Lost Boys, which opened last season, also continues to draw in crowds, edging out past favorites including Wicked, which has seen its grosses gradually drop throughout 2026.

New musical Wanted opened on Nov. 8 to mixed reviews. In the heavily comped week in the leadup, as well as the fully comped opening night, the show brought in $517,134 and played to 94 percent capacity.

Several shows were in previews last week, including Downstate, and The Fanstasticks. Here There Are Blueberries began previews last week, with 99 percent capacity and $669,084 across seven performances. Holiday radio play It’s a Wonderful Life, starring Andrew Rannells, Megan Hilty, Tituss Burgess, Lisa Rinna and Harry Hamlin, played its first six performances last week. The show had a somewhat shaky start with 78 percent capacity and a gross of $322,788.10.

Overall the industry gross rose 24 percent and attendance 15 percent thanks to the addition of the two new shows, as well as the rebound from Halloween and marathon weekend.

#794. The 23 Best Christmas Gifts for Parents to Shop Online in 2026

Cheers to another year of being the best gift giver in the family — we won't take credit.

All products and services featured are independently chosen by editors. However, Billboard may receive a commission on orders placed through its retail links, and the retailer may receive certain auditable data for accounting purposes.

Parents are arguably the hardest to shop gifts for, because their answer usually boils down to “I don’t need anything” or “It’s up to you.” There are endless options, and it could be overwhelming for someone who wants to be the favorite child slash gift giver to the people who gave them life. Explore Billboard See latest videos, charts and news

Mars Global Surveyor looked at the south pole of Mars and saw signs of possible climate change.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 7, 1996, NASA launched its Mars Global Surveyor mission. This was the first mission NASA sent to Mars in almost 20 years!

The Mars Global Surveyor spacecraft was an orbiter. It transmitted data from NASA's Mars rovers Sojourner, Spirit and Opportunity back to Earth. The spacecraft also did a lot of its own science. It found surface channels on Mars that appeared to have been created by running water.

Mars Global Surveyor looked at the south pole of Mars and saw signs of possible climate change. It also saw a mineral called hematite on Mars. Hematite usually forms in water. NASA then sent its Spirit and Opportunity rovers to look for the hematite, and both rovers found it near their landing sites.

Mars Global Surveyor survived much longer than expected. But a space maneuver accidentally exposed one of its batteries to the sun, and the spacecraft lost power. It fell silent forever in November 2006.

As the first successful Mars mission since the two Viking launches in 1975, Mars Global Surveyor ushered in a new era of exploration of the Red Planet, not only through its own contributions to orbit-based science, but by serving a relay for surface-based rovers. As such, it became a primary pipeline for multiple concurrent Mars missions."The [Mars Global Surveyor] mission overhauled scientists' understanding of Mars by studying the entire Martian surface, atmosphere and interior. Major findings included dramatic evidence that water still flows on Mars in short bursts down hillside gullies, and the identification of water-related mineral deposits leading to selection of a Mars rover landing site for a subsequent mission," read a NASA description of the probe.

Mars Global Surveyor sent back more than 240,000 images to Earth during its nine active years.Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube.

In her spare time, Hanneke enjoys exploring the Rocky Mountains, basking in nature and looking for dark skies to gaze at the cosmos.

#792. Brenda Song Says She Felt “Underpaid and Overworked” on Disney’s ‘The Suite Life’ Shows

"I feel like there are parts of the 'Suite Life' that are, like, black holes for me. Like, I don’t remember years of my life," Song said while speaking with her former co-star, Dylan Sprouse.

Brenda Song is reflecting on her time as a child actor, admitting that she felt “underpaid and overworked” while working on Disney‘s The Suite Life shows.

The Running Point star appeared on her former co-star Dylan Sprouse‘s Wildmen podcast, where they recalled working on The Suite Life of Zack & Cody franchise for Disney, and its subsequent spinoff The Suite Life on Deck.

“I’ve been curious to ask you about this,” Song said to Sprouse. “I feel like there are parts of the Suite Life that are, like, black holes for me. Like, I don’t remember years of my life.” Related Stories TV 'Frozen' Is Getting the 'A Real Bug's Life' Treatment With Nat Geo, Disney+ and Hulu's 'The Real Frozen' Movies Watch Disney's Holiday Short 'The Invisible Horse' From 'Paddington in Peru' Director Dougal Wilson

Wildmen co-host Brendan Columbus recounted a recent episode of the podcast they did with Phill Lewis, noting, “Phill said he forgot directing episodes. It was like, he’s like, ‘They’re just gone.’ He’ll watch them again. Just have no recollection.”

Song said looking back on her time on the Disney Channel series, it felt like “we paid them.” She added, “I always say this about my time at Disney, I know everybody has their own journey… I always say, like, I have a boring tale. I didn’t have this crazy, like, ‘Oh my God, this was so — I had a lovely time.”

The actress admitted that “the only thing that was hard about that time was I feel like we were underpaid and overworked.” Song added, “But Disney did give us a platform to be sitting here right now, so it’s very hard to complain about certain things.”

The Hollywood Reporter reached out to Disney for comment, but did not hear back.

The Sprouse twins starred in Disney’s Suite Life shows as onscreen twins Cody and Zack Martin who lived in the Tipton Hotel. Song starred as London Tipton, daughter of hotel owner Wilfred Tipton; Lewis portrayed Marion Moseby, the manager of the hotel. Ashley Tisdale also starred in the show as Maddie Fitzpatrick, London’s friend and a Tipton Hotel employee.

Sprouse recently revealed on his podcast that he’s received only one residual check for five cents from his time working on The Suite Life of Zack & Cody.

“The only residual check I’ve ever received for The Suite Life at all was a crossover episode with Hannah Montana for five cents. I’m not joking,” he said. “Imagine that. In a time where residuals would have been great, not a single paycheck for being arguably one of the most popular shows.”

During that same episode of Sprouse’s podcast, he and Phill Lewis recalled shooting “wraparound episodes,” in which they’d film an additional scene from a future episode each week.

“A wraparound episode was we’d shoot our episode for the week and then they would say, ‘OK, we’re going to shoot this scene from an episode that you’re going to shoot in two weeks,’ and we’re like, ‘OK.’ So we shoot that scene. Then the next week they go, ‘You’re gonna shoot this scene from the same ep.’ And what they were doing was they were compiling an episode by shooting a scene a week, and then putting it together.”

When asked if it “counted” as a new episode, Sprouse said, “Not for us!” Lewis alleged, “We didn’t get paid for it. We weren’t paid for that episode.”

#791. Jill Scott & Kehlani Face Off In Crowded R&B Album Category at 2027 Grammys: Our Predictions

At the 2026 Grammys, Leon Thomas emerged victorious in the best R&B album category, fending off fellow nominees GIVĒON (Beloved), Ledisi (The Crown), Teyana Taylor (Escape Room) and Coco Jones (Why Not More?). With a Billboard Hot 100 top 10 hit (“Mutt”) and a near-perfect campaign under his belt, the award was practically Thomas’ to lose. But this year’s field is a lot more competitive.

Three-time Grammy-winning R&B icon Jill Scott is the frontrunner for best R&B album at the 2027 Grammys. To Whom This May Concern, her first full-length offering in 11 years, debuted in the top 10 of seven different Billboard charts, spawned her first Adult R&B Airplay chart-topper in over a decade (“Pressha”) and gave way to an acclaimed headlining tour.

Scott, who was inducted into Billboard’s R&B Hall of Fame earlier this year, will likely be nominated across the R&B field, with select album tracks having non-zero chances of showing up in the rap and American roots categories. She’s been incredibly visible this year — even reprising her iconic role of Sheila Jackson in Why Did I Get Married Again? — but, more importantly, Concern is one of the year’s best albums. In fact, Scott may well break into the general field with an album of the year nomination: At least one R&B album has made the lineup every year this decade except for 2025, and Scott fits the bill of a respected OG who delivered a project that met the moment with a career-redefining album.

Kehlani, who won best R&B song and performance last year for her Hot 100 top 10 hit “Folded” (No. 6), is neck-and-neck with Scott for a nomination here. Her self-titled set reached No. 4 on the Billboard 200 and No. 1 on Top R&B/Hip-Hop Albums. Featuring icons like Brandy and Missy Elliott, the set also spawned the Usher-assisted hit “Shoulda Never,” which reached No. 10 on Mainstream R&B/Hip-Hop Airplay. The Oakland singer has re-established herself as a Grammy darling in recent years (she picked up three nods at the 2025 ceremony after a seven-year absence), and she’s also a frontrunner to win best melodic rap performance this year alongside Cardi B for “Safe.”

PJ Morton is currently the male soloist with the most nominations in this category (four), and he’s poised to extend that lead with Saturday Night, the R&B side of his Juneteenth-released double album. Chris Brown could potentially become the male soloist with the second-most nods in this category if he makes the final lineup with Brown (The Chocolate Edition). He won here just two years ago for 11:11 (Deluxe), but that album had the hits, acclaim and passion that Brown — which Pitchfork infamously scored a 1.3 out of 10 — lacks. Working in Brown’s favor is his stadium-conquering joint R&B Tour with Usher, which has reinforced his status as one of the most lucrative touring acts in Black music history. Nonetheless, the rumored, concert-delaying tension between the two stars, coupled with Brown’s recent multimillion-dollar legal battle with his former housekeeper, could turn off voters.

Enter a trio of acts that could become first-time nominees in this category: Masego, The Womack Sisters and Kenyon Dixon. Masego made a grand return with Fix Your Face, his first album in three years, which had minimal chart impact but won lots of love in R&B circles thanks to his headlining tour, his Herbie Hancock-honoring “Recommend” music video and standout cuts like “Breathe,” “Heaven” and “Hello” (with Buju Banton). The Womack Sisters, a girl group consisting of siblings who are the nieces of Bobby Womack and granddaughters of Sam Cooke, could earn a nod here for their self-titled debut studio album. The focus single “If I Let You” has reached No. 11 on Adult Alternative Airplay, and the trio is set to open for select dates on Harry Styles’ stadium-headlining Together, Together tour next spring. Finally, Kenyon Dixon, a five-time Grammy nominee, is seeking his first nod in this category for Ego Ruins Everything. He’s garnered tons of love from more traditional R&B fans (his first three career Grammy nods were all for best traditional R&B performance), and Ego elegantly blends more contemporary flourishes into his soulful sound.

Three ladies who helped define late-2010s and early-2020s R&B also have albums in contention: Ella Mai has only scored one nod in this category, but she could return with Do You Still Love Me?, which spawned the Hot 100 hit “Little Things” (No. 81) and anchored her headlining tour. Similarly, Summer Walker boasts one previous nomination in this category, but it was for her Clear 2: Soft Life EP, which offered a far more stripped-down sound than the radio-ready Finally Over It. Nonetheless, the conclusion to the Atlanta singer’s Over It trilogy posted the biggest Billboard 200 debut by a female R&B artist in 2025, dominated the set list of its accompanying arena-headlining tour and spawned several Hot 100 hits, including “Go Girl” (No. 60), “Robbed You” (No. 58) and “No” (No. 69). Then again, her campaign could be stunted by her ongoing legal dispute with Interscope. Finally, Ari Lennox has inexplicably never earned a Grammy nomination for her own work (her sole nod came from Dreamville’s 2020 best rap album bid for Revenge of the Dreamers III), but she could finally make it happen with Vacancy. The record reached No. 25 on Top R&B Albums and earned considerable acclaim in R&B circles.

Mariah Carey is one legend to look out for. She’s in contention with Here for It All, an album that reached the Billboard 200 top 10 (No. 7), spawned two Adult R&B Airplay chart-toppers in “In Your Feelings” and “Type Dangerous,” and housed “Nothing Is Impossible,” which she performed at the 2026 Milan Cortina Winter Olympics Opening Ceremony. With just five wins across her decade-spanning career, Carey is far from a Grammy darling; she hasn’t been recognized by the Recording Academy since 2009, and R&B voters haven’t awarded her since 2006, when she took home best contemporary R&B album for The Emancipation of Mimi and best female R&B vocal performance for “We Belong Together.”

Other titles to look out for include: Heat the Streets (Elmiene), Love Me for Me (October London), God Must Really Love Me (Tori Kelly), Juniper (Joy Crookes), Eric Bellinger (Eric Bellinger) and Ghosted (Saint Harison)

We’re predicting: To Whom This May Concern (Jill Scott); Kehlani (Kehlani); Fix Your Face (Masego); Saturday Night (PJ Morton); The Womack Sisters (The Womack Sisters)

#788. California votes to give record $8.4 billion to medical research

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Students, researchers and others at the University of California, Los Angeles, have protested over cuts to science funding made by the administration of US President Donald Trump during the past two years.Credit: Robyn Beck/AFP via Getty

Voters in California have approved US$8.4 billion in funding for immunology research — the largest ever infusion of cash for science authorized by a public vote in US history.

The funding proposal, known as Proposition 38, appeared on the ballot for voters in California in last week’s US mid-term elections, but it has taken nearly a week for officials to count enough ballots to declare its success. The state government will pay for the research — which aims to find treatments that harness or re-engineer the body’s immune system to fight illnesses such as cancer and Alzheimer’s disease — by selling state government bonds. (This is unusual for science funding. Bonds are typically reserved to pay for infrastructure projects such as road construction and require the state to pay back its debt with interest.)

‘Historic change’: what the 2026 US mid-term election results mean for science

‘Historic change’: what the 2026 US mid-term election results mean for science

Supporters of the proposal say that the funding will provide stability for researchers in California, who have been affected by political turmoil. The administration of US President Donald Trump has pushed for massive cuts to science funding; put political appointees in charge of grant decisions at federal science agencies, such as the US National Institutes of Health; and forced policy change at US universities that receive federal funding, including those in California.

The $8.4 billion “is an advantage to California that is unprecedented”, says Antoni Ribas, a cancer researcher and physician at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), who supported Proposition 38. It will make the state “even more of a global hub for immunology research”.

But the proposal has sparked debate. That’s because it calls for giving about half of the funding directly to research institutes — and the only institute that matches the criteria called for in the proposal is one co-founded by Gary Michelson, a billionaire medical-device inventor. He wrote the proposition and donated about $45 million of his own funds to get it placed on the ballot and to campaign for its passage.

“I feel like the voters have been taken advantage of,” says Sarah Hill, a political scientist at California State University, Fullerton, who tracks the state’s ballot measures. Michelson did not respond to Nature’s request for comment before this story was published, but has said elsewhere that he will not personally profit from the bond revenue.

In California, citizens can place proposed laws directly on the election ballot by collecting hundreds of thousands of voter signatures.

The state has funded scientific research through this process before. In 2004, after then-president George W. Bush restricted federal funding for human embryonic stem-cell research, voters in California approved a $3-billion bond to establish the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine, which they then voted to replenish with another $5.5 billion in 2020.

A campaign mailer encouraging California voters to support Proposition 38.Credit: Smith Collection/Gado/Getty

“The model works,” Ribas says. Immunologists have been making great strides with medicines, such as personalized treatments called CAR-T therapies, that are revolutionizing care, he says. There has also been a flurry of research into developing vaccines, such as the mRNA shots that have been the target of funding cuts by the Trump administration. Proposition 38 will ensure such research can continue regardless of the political headwinds, Ribas adds.

Around $4 billion from Proposition 38 will fund grants for researchers at select public universities and non-profit institutes in California through a competitive review process. According to the proposal, any commercialized therapies developed through funded research must be sold at a 20% discount to people in California, with 10% of drug royalties returning to the state’s general fund.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03635-6

#787. Nicko McBrain on Iron Maiden Missing Its Rock Hall Induction: ‘I’m Sure We’ll Say Thank You In Another Way’

The drummer, who recently retired from the road, is releasing his memoir, Hello Boys and Girls!, ahead of the ceremony.

In his new memoir, Nicko McBrain joyfully cracks open the tight, closed world that is Iron Maiden. And while there’s plenty of metal in its 344 pages, don’t expect to find much in the way of mayhem in Hello Boys and Girls! (HarperCollins), publishing just in front of the band’s induction into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame on Saturday (Nov. 14). Explore Iron Maiden See latest videos, charts and news

“I intentionally steered away from the debauchery; there’s a fair share in there, but I wanted it to be more classy, this story,” the London-born drummer — who joined Maiden during 1982 and retired from touring with the band in December 2024 — tells Billboard via Zoom from his home in Boca Raton, Fla. “We were very young, very proud, very crazy. There were a lot of drugs. The sex, we had our fair share – yeah, we did — but I didn’t want the book to reflect that. I wanted it to be more passionate, more reflective of the story rather than going into the gutter…’cause we weren’t in it for the sex and drugs and the money. That was never the drive and the passion behind Iron Maiden, and it’s the same today.” Related Bella Kay Teases New Music In Billboard 'Up & Coming' Podcast Series Premiere: 'It's Kinda Giving Deluxe' It's Looking Like Oasis Will Skip Their Own Rock Hall of Fame Induction: 'It's Too Far To Be Going For the Night' Brothers Osborne, Luke Bryan, Vince Gill, Halestorm & More Added As 2026 CMA Awards Performers

McBrain adds, “You have to bear in mind that (now) everybody is married and has their own families and children who, goodness gracious, are all grown up. So I steered clear, intentionally, of most of the stories that involved the debauchery.” He adds with a laugh that “there are certain stories to be told. Maybe that’ll be another book!”

All that said, Hello Boys and Girls! is still an entertaining and engaging rock ‘n’ roll read. Co-written with Benjamin Dirs (Geezer Butler’s Into the Void), it captures McBrain’s jovial and conversational demeanor and outlook, laughing at the world around him — and often at himself. It also illuminates how a youngster blown away by Dave Brubeck Quartet drummer Joe Morello’s “Take Five” solo on the BBC became a career player himself.

That includes several eventful stops before McBain made it into Maiden in 1982 — including sessions for guitarist Gordon Giltrap and membership in Streetwalkers, Pat Travers’ band and the French group Trust, whose frequent food fights, on any occasion and any locale, provide some of the book’s funniest moments.

“I thought the main reason to write this story was because there’s so much that happened prior to Iron Maiden,” he says, “With great bands, players and musicians. So the inspiration was all of the stories prior to Maiden, and then we get to the nitty-gritty stuff. But it isn’t a book just about my lifetime spent in the ranks of Iron Maiden — 42 years, that’s a long time and a blessing as well. But the inspiration was I wanted to write my story about my life, and of course the majority of it is Iron Maiden stories.”

One thing that’s abundantly clear in Hello Boys and Girls! is that, alongside wife Rebecca — whom McBrain calls “my true north star” in the dedication — drums are, in fact, the love of his life.

“Absolutely,” he acknowledges. “I think it was the ferocity, the voracious stamina that (Morello) had when I saw that solo. I was 10 and a half years old. The ‘Take Five’ groove in itself, I’d never heard anything like that, in the odd time. I always thought 1-2-3-4, 2-2-3-4…So hearing a 5/4 drum fill and the music being played, I’m like, ‘What is this?’ Then he went off into the solo, and I’m like, ‘That’s what I want to do, dad! I’m gonna be a drummer!'”

McBrain says the book has been a long time coming. He had a publishing deal more than dozen years ago and was 20 or so chapters in when he “hit a brick wall” — partly due to Maiden commitments — and elected to give his advance payment back. But when he decided to retire after suffering a stroke in 2023, the band’s management revived the idea and helped him move the project forward. Maiden bassist and founder Steve Harris, he says, was also encouraging. “I took away a humbleness while I was writing,” McBrain says. “The whole time I thought, ‘Be humble, mate. Just tell the story.’ I was told off about a couple of things by (manager Rod Smallwood) — ‘Oh, no, you can’t be writing about that’ and I went, ‘Sorry, Rod; this is my story.'”

Hello Boys and Girls! follows Maiden guitarist Adrian Smith’s 2020 Monsters of River and Rock, which dealt as much with his passion for fishing as it did music. As of this interview, McBrain is waiting for Maiden members’ reactions to his book.

“I’m not sure if any of the band has seen it; I think if they have I’ll be getting a bollocking, a phone call: ‘You shouldn’t be saying that!'” he says with another laugh. “I think Steve might have had a little look at it, but I haven’t actually spoken to him about it. When the speaking tour I’m doing  all sold out, he sent me a note: ‘Well done. Congratulations. Knock ’em dead.'”

Nearly two years after his final concert with the group, McBrain — who now plays in a Maiden tribute band called Titanium Tart — says that “I dearly miss the camaraderie of my brothers every day. I don’t miss the travel (but) I miss the fans, the interaction at a live show and the interaction on the days off when Janick (Gers, guitarist) and I would have a wander around the city we were in and get to see the fans and meet them. I miss that. I miss the crew. And I miss the feeling of sitting behind my drum set and playing and driving the band.” But he’s had no second thoughts or regrets about his decision.

“I am grateful and praise God every day for giving me this wonderful life I’ve had,” says McBrain, adding that he’s in good health — “just normal aches and pains of being an old git” — and taking “proactive” care of himself since the stroke. He has not seen Iron Maiden live since he retired, partly in deference to current touring drummer Simon Dawson (from Harris’ other band, British Lion). McBrain says he hopes “to do a couple of songs” on the next Maiden album, though there are no concrete plans yet for a follow-up to 2021’s Senjutsu, which became their highest-charting album on the Billboard 200 upon its release.

“Because of my handicap, it would have to be a song like ‘Stranger in a Strange Land’ or ‘Number of the Beast,'” McBrain says, “Something that’s not got large drum fills and drum motifs in them, ’cause I wouldn’t be able to play them. I went to dinner with Bruce (Dickinson, frontman) last year and I said, ‘Are you gonna do a new record?’ and he looked at me and said, ‘What do you think?’ Knowing Bruce, that’s what he wants. And I did talk to Steve, and it was like, ‘Maybe.’ So at this moment there’s no plans to do a new record, but watch this space, ironmaiden.com. That’s all I can say.”

McBrain says he was willing to represent Maiden at the Rock Hall induction in Los Angeles while the band tours Australia, but his speaking tour in Europe, which kicked off Oct. 26 in Germany, will keep him across the pond through early December. (He’s also added a Dec. 8 appearance at the Barnes & Noble store in Boca Raton, Fla.) He’s nevertheless “personally very honored” by the induction, despite Maiden’s professed ambivalence about the institution.

“It’s taken a long time for the band to be recognized,” McBrain says. “There was a time when I agreed with Bruce and said, ‘This is a load of kerfuffle. We don’t even want to entertain thinking about it.’ That was way back; now we’re moving forward, and there have been changes within the powers that be and I think they’re more listening to what the fans want. Now, I think to have an accolade and be honored like that, it’s great. I would’ve gone in a heartbeat, but I’m on tour and the boys are in Australia. I’m sure we’ll say thank you in another way.”

McBrain’s remaining author appearances include:

Nov. 13 — DR Studio 2, Copenhagen, Denmark

Nov. 15 — Malta Music Festival, St. Julian’s, Malta

Dec. 8 — Barnes & Noble, Boca Raton, Fla.

Life can leave its mark on a planetary atmosphere, so learning what properties are the product of non-life will help astronomers identify those worlds that might have life.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A new computer simulation that depicts Earth, or a rocky planet in general, without life is the latest tool in the quest to discover whether or not we are alone in the universe.

Life leaves its mark on a planet, particularly its atmosphere, in the form of a mixture of biochemically created gases. Some are obvious, while others can be produced by both biology and geology, meaning that distinguishing a planet that has life from one that does not, solely based on what gases we can detect in its atmosphere, can be difficult. The key is in knowing which atmospheric conditions can be explained without life.

To aid in distinguishing between habitable and inhabited planets, planetary scientist Samantha Gilbert-Janizek of the University of California, Riverside, developed a model that simulates the evolution of a rocky planet without life.

"The model can help us see how habitable but non-living planets might mimic living planets," Gilbert-Janizek, who was a PhD student at the University of Washington when the research was conducted, said in a statement.

Gilbert-Janizek built upon a model previously developed by Washington’s Rory Barnes that simulated the core, mantle, and crust of a planet. This new model pushed the simulation two steps further by incorporating the surface and atmosphere of the planet as well.

In all, the model simulates 19 properties of a rocky planet that are not related to life, including the amount of heat a planet receives from its star, the exchange of heat and chemicals from the core to the surface, and the outflow of certain gases from the subsurface.

Gilbert-Janizek’s starting point was to simulate the development of Earth had life never arisen here, therefore providing a baseline with which to compare to exoplanets. She ran the simulation from the birth of Earth 4.5 billion years ago to 500 million years into the future. The result was a lifeless world, but one that still had oceans and an atmosphere.

"When we interpret observations of an exoplanet’s atmosphere, this tool will help us determine the probability that what we observe indicates life on the surface," said Gilbert-Janizek.

What makes the simulation especially useful is its plug-and-play nature. Researchers can simply apply the bulk properties of whichever planet they are studying to the model, and then just let it run. If the result is a planet with an atmosphere that matches what is detected spectroscopically by the James Webb Space Telescope or, in the future, the various extremely large 30-meter-plus ground-based telescopes or NASA’s planned Habitable Worlds Observatory, then we know that planet probably does not have life as we know it.

However, if the simulated planet without life does not match what we observe on the real planet, then it becomes possible that life is present and altering the atmosphere.

"Dr Gilbert-Janizek’s work represents an exciting step toward understanding where life can exist in the universe,” said Barnes. "After more than a decade of work by many scientists, Dr Gilbert-Janizek has finally completed a model of the Earth that simultaneously reproduces properties of Earth’s core, mantle, surface and atmosphere. That calibration gives us confidence that future simulations of exoplanets will be accurate."

While any deviation from what is predicted by the model will not necessarily mean there is definitely life on a planet, it will help pick out those worlds that are worthy of follow-up studies by the next generation of telescopes.

Gilbert-Janizek’s model is described in a paper published in The Planetary Science Journal.

Keith Cooper is a freelance science journalist and editor in the United Kingdom, and has a degree in physics and astrophysics from the University of Manchester. He's the author of "The Contact Paradox: Challenging Our Assumptions in the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence" (Bloomsbury Sigma, 2020) and has written articles on astronomy, space, physics and astrobiology for a multitude of magazines and websites.

The three-headed Kaiju's origins aren't just space-based; one of the largest structures in the universe shares its name.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Godzilla goes toe-to-toe with long-time foe King Ghidorah in Godzilla Minus Zero, which opened in theaters on Friday (Nov. 6). Though the three-headed golden Kaiju might seem like a natural native of Monster Island, King Ghidorah actually emerged from the depths of space.

However, it isn't just the origins of King Ghidorah — also known as Monster Zero in the Godzilla movie Invasion of Astro-Monster (1965) — that are this beast's only cosmic connection. One of the largest structures in the universe, the King Ghidorah Supercluster, was named in honor of Godzilla's primary antagonist.

King Ghidorah is a three-headed, twin-tailed golden dragon from the stars, first introduced in the fifth Godzilla movie, Ghidorah, the Three-Headed Monster (1964).

In this first appearance, part of the Shōwa era (1964–1975) of Godzilla history, Ghidorah ravaged Venus, wiping out its population 5,000 years before arriving on Earth encased within a highly magnetic meteorite. Ghidorah was bested this first time by Godzilla, Rodan, and Mothra.

Undeterred, Ghidorah returned for a rematch just a year later in Invasion of Astro Monster (1965), after being discovered supposedly terrorizing the inhabitants of Planet X, a world found beyond Jupiter. In this movie, it is revealed that Ghidorah is less a king and more a pawn, under the control of calculating Xiliens as part of a plan to subjugate Earth. This will become a theme.

Freed from that control, Ghidorah returns to deep space, once again falling under the thrall of an alien race in 1968's Destroy All Monsters.This movie sees Ghidorah hold its own against a who's who of kaiju, eventually succumbing to the combined might of Godzilla, Minilla, Mothra, Rodan, Manda, Gorosaurus, Anguirus, Kumonga, Baragon, and Varan.

Even with three gravity-beam-blasting heads, that is hardly fair!

Ghidorah returned with some backup for a final time in the Shōwa era in 1975's Godzilla vs. Gigan. This time, Ghidorah and his tag-team partner Gigan (who resembled a giant one-eyed space chicken) were under the control of cockroach-like Nebulans. Getting mind-controlled three times is just embarrassing!

Fortunately, the Shōwa era drew to a close in 1975 before Ghidorah was forced into servitude for a fourth time.

Ghidorah returned in the rebooted Godzilla timeline of the Heisei era (1991–1998) in 1991's Godzilla Vs. King Ghidorah, but its cosmic origins are gone. The Heisei Ghidorah begins life as three genetically engineered creatures called Dorats in the future before being morphed into a three-headed form via nuclear exposure.

Ghidorah was given a spiritual origin in the Millennium era's Godzilla, Mothra, and King Ghidorah: Giant Monsters All-Out Attack (2001), actually serving as a protagonist, helping Mothra in halting Godzilla's rampage.

Ghidorah is once again an extraterrestrial in Universal Pictures' MonsterVerse movie Godzilla: King of the Monsters (2019), being described as having "fallen from the stars" in ancient times before rising to challenge Godzilla.

Now King Ghidorah is back once again in Godzilla Minus Zero, maintaining his extraterrestrial origin story and once again challenging Godzilla to an epic kaiju battle. Those are some of the fictional versions of this golden beast, but what does it look like in reality?

Arguably the most impressive feat of King Ghidorah has been to make itself such an important part of pop culture that astronomers took note. The King Ghidorah supercluster is a collection of galaxies located around 6.7 billion light-years from Earth. Covering an area of the sky equivalent to 19 full moons, as seen from our vantage point, this cosmic Kaiju was discovered in late 2022 by Japanese astronomers using data from the Subaru Telescope.

The King Ghidorah supercluster is comprised of at least 19 individual associated galaxy clusters. It stretches out for an incredible 1.3 billion light-years, meaning the entire Milky Way could fit across it around 12,300 times. That makes it the largest supercluster ever discovered.

To put into context just how monstrous the King Ghidorah supercluster is, consider the fact that it has a mass equivalent to 10,000,000,000,000,000 suns, 10 times as massive as the Milky Way's home supercluster, Laniakea. Even Godzilla may think twice before attempting to tussle with that particular King Ghidorah!

See King Ghidorah in action in Godzilla Minus Zero, which is showing in theaters in the US and UK from November 6. You can see the preceding movie, Godzilla Minus One, on Netflix.

Venus Express had to survive harsh radiation at Venus, but it persevered for nine years.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 8, 2005, Europe launched its first mission to Venus. The spacecraft was called Venus Express.

Venus is a hothouse planet, one where the atmospheric pressure can easily crush an unprotected spacecraft. Even from orbit, Venus Express had to survive harsh radiation. But the spacecraft lasted for more than nine years.

During that time, Venus Express saw a weird vortex swirling around Venus's south pole. It also saw possible signs of active volcanoes. Venus Express also discovered that the planet generates its own auroras. These auroras happen when particles from the sun hit charged particles in the atmosphere.

Late in the Venus Express mission, controllers told the spacecraft to dip down into Venus's clouds — even though the spacecraft wasn't designed to do this. It performed well, but eventually it stopped listening to commands. The spacecraft burned up in the atmosphere in January 2015.

Venus Express established ESA as the third world organization to successfully send a probe to study Venus, following the United States and Soviet Union. (Japan's JAXA became the fourth five years later.)

"By studying Venus, scientists learn how Earth-like planets change over time," reads a summary of the planet's exploration prepared by The Planetary Society. "Orbital studies [like Venus Express] hint that Venus may have hosted habitable oceans before becoming inhospitable."

"By studying Venus, we can learn how Earth-like planets evolve and what shapes planets throughout the galaxy into temperate, lush worlds instead of sweltering hothouses. Venus also helps scientists model Earth’s climate, and may serve as a cautionary tale on how dramatically a planet’s climate can change," wrote the Society.

ESA returned to Venus in 2018 when BepiColombo, its joint mission with JAXA, used the planet's gravity to redirect its path toward the planet Mercury.

#781. Nothing to Cluck At: Goldie Hawn Recalls Wacky Thing Elvis Presley Said She Looked Like When They First Met

All the actress could do at the time was say "thank you."

Goldie Hawn’s first interaction with Elvis Presley was memorable, to say the least — and not just because she was in the presence of the King of Rock & Roll.

While appearing on The Jennifer Hudson Show on Tuesday (Nov. 10), the actress opened up about crossing paths with Presley while rehearsing Laugh-In many decades ago at NBC Studios. “I remember I was wearing a purple wool jumpsuit, and I went over to him and I said hi,” Hawn began.

“He took my hair and went, ‘You look like a chicken that’s just been hatched,'” she said, making Jennifer Hudson’s jaw drop. “I said, ‘Oh, thank you.'”

A few years later, Hawn would headline a residency at the Hilton Hotel in Las Vegas, where Presley was kind enough to invite her to stay in his private suite. “He didn’t let a lot of people back there,” she recalled to Hudson. “But me and my daddy [Edward Rutledge Hawn], we stayed in his big suite. … I was there for three weeks. And I saw [Elvis] during that time and he was a precious, precious person.”

Also on the talk show, the Death Becomes Her star spoke about her new children’s book The After-School Kindness Crew (Pooch on the Loose #1), which was published this past May. Hawn shared her passion for kids’ literature with late friend and Imagination Library founder Dolly Parton, whom the Hollywood legend honored in August after the country superstar passed away at the age of 80.

“She was a ray of light!” Hawn wrote on Instagram at the time. “She was lit up like an angel, a joyful, celestial being. Dolly blessed us all for generations to come. Rest, dear Angel, and, as you said, keep the angels creating music and singing in the heavens.”

"Starlog" was one of the greatest sci-fi and fantasy magazines ever, and after a 17-year absence, it's being resurrected.

The legendary sci-fi mag went dark back in 2009 as part of the wave of popular publications folding due to years of declining readership and subscriptions. But as of Nov. 13, this geek favorite periodical returns as an annual print edition, and it's available for pre-order now.

It’s another indication of digital fatigue in the world, and fans of a certain age will recall the pleasure of poring over each colorful issue packed with in-depth interviews, behind-the-scenes photos, TV guides, classic movie retrospectives, book reviews, con news, and VFX features.

"Starlog" launched in 1976, in the pre-"Star Wars" days, under the leadership of editor-in-chief Kerry O’Quinn. It first arrived with artist Jack Thurston's beautiful painted "Star Trek" cover, featuring William Shatner as Captain James T. Kirk and Leonard Nimoy’s Spock, set against the U.S.S. Enterprise near a shimmering black hole.

The magazine continued to inform the science fiction community about upcoming sci-fi TV shows and blockbuster Hollywood films for over three decades; I fondly recall reading each informative and entertaining monthly issue cover-to-cover.

Just in time to honor its 50th anniversary this year, "Starlog" blasts back into the sci-fi universe with Issue #375 showcasing cover artwork created by Armenian artist Gabriel Yeganyan. Its geek culture legacy, covering iconic franchises like "Star Wars," "Star Trek," and "Alien," will now live on thanks to Fangoria Holdings and io9 co-founder Annalee Newitz, editor-in-chief.

"During its original 33-year run, 'Starlog' documented science fiction as it evolved across film, television, books, technology, and culture," said 'Fangoria's Tara Ansley.

"Fifty years after the magazine first launched, the line between science fiction and the real world has become increasingly difficult to separate. That makes this an especially interesting time to bring 'Starlog' back. Technology may change, but the most compelling questions have always been about people: how we live, what we create, and what kind of future we want to build."

"Starlog" reloads for its first annual edition after a long hiatus on Nov. 13. You can pre-order the first issue (Issue 375 in continuity) on the Starlog website.

Jeff Spry is an award-winning screenwriter and veteran freelance journalist covering TV, movies, video games, books, and comics. His work has appeared at SYFY Wire, Inverse, Collider, Bleeding Cool and elsewhere. Jeff lives in beautiful Bend, Oregon amid the ponderosa pines, classic muscle cars, a crypt of collector horror comics, and two loyal English Setters.

#777. Michael Jackson’s ‘Thriller’ Scares Up 40th Week at No. 1 on Top R&B/Hip-Hop Albums Chart

The set's title track sparks gains for the landmark album after its annual Halloween surge.

For the second time this year, Michael Jackson’s landmark album Thriller glides to the top of the Top R&B/Hip-Hop Albums chart after a mass pop-culture moment.

Unlike the wider spring and summer cycle sparked from the Michael biopic, the latest surge largely centers on one song, the album’s title track, after gains from the Halloween holiday.

Thriller, on the Epic/Legacy record labels, tops the chart dated Nov. 14, rising three spots to crown the list. For its latest coronation, the set earned 55,000 equivalent album units for the Oct. 29 – Nov. 5 tracking week, according to Luminate, an 89% improvement from 29,000 units in the week prior.

Streaming activity contributed 32,000 units of the sum (a figure representing 34.2 million official on-demand streams of the album’s songs), traditional album sums provided 22,000 units and 1,000 units were from track-equivalent album units. (One unit equals the following levels of consumption: one album sale, 10 individual tracks sold from an album, or 1,000 paid/subscription tier or 2,500 ad-supported tier official on-demand audio and video streams for a song on the album.)

With its return, Thriller achieves a 40th week at No. 1 on Top R&B/Hip-Hop Albums, following two weeks at No. 1 in May in the wake of post-Michael mania. The landmark 1982 release, often cited as the best-selling album of all time, held the record for most weeks at No. 1 on the chart from 1984 until 2025, when SZA’s SOS took the title. Thriller narrows the gap with SOS, which remains in first place with 46 weeks on top, having most recently topped the ranking in January.

Here’s a review of the longest leaders on Top R&B/Hip-Hop Albums:

46, SOS, SZA, 2022-2640, Thriller, Michael Jackson, 1983-84; 202629, Please Hammer Don’t Hurt ‘Em, M.C. Hammer, 199026, Just Like the First Time, Freddie Jackson, 1986-8723, Can’t Slow Down, Lionel Richie, 1983-8420, Songs in the Key of Life, Stevie Wonder, 1976-7720, Street Songs, Rick James, 198120, Shoot for the Stars Aim for the Moon, Pop Smoke, 2020-21

Additionally, Thriller’s new frame gives the King of Pop a 101st career week at No. 1 on Top R&B/Hip-Hop Albums, the second-most of all acts since the chart’s launch in 1965. He trails only former Motown labelmates The Temptations, who have posted a record 109 weeks in the penthouse.

Elsewhere, Thriller crowns the Top R&B Albums chart for an 18th week with a 3-1 ascent, while it races 13-2 on the all-genre Billboard 200. On the latter, it achieves its highest rank since 1984, the year it wrapped its 37 weeks atop the list, the most for an album by a single artist.

#776. sombr Pleads With Concertgoer to Stop Flipping Him Off: ‘It’s Really Making Me Sad, Man’

"I don't appreciate it," the singer said. "This is a safe space."

One person’s rude gestures in the crowd at sombr‘s recent concert made the musician feel, well, somber.

As captured in clips from the night, the pop star paused his Sunday show in Columbus, Ohio, to express his dismay over a man in attendance who apparently wouldn’t stop giving sombr the middle finger while he was performing. “[He] just keeps flipping me off and flipping me off every night,” the singer/songwriter said.

“Man, I don’t know why you’re coming to my concert if you’re gonna keep flipping me off,” he continued. “It’s all love, but please, please don’t flip me off at my show. It’s this guy with the shades and the leather jacket right here. … It’s really making me sad, man. I don’t appreciate it. This is a safe space. I want everyone here to be kind to each other.”

It’s unclear if sombr and the culprit were able to go back to friends after the exchange, but in general, the hitmaker has had his share of experience dealing with negativity. He previously made headlines when he defended himself against a person who posted a viral TikTok bashing his concert performance and appearance, and in September, sombr passed along the advice Taylor Swift gave him on the subject.

“One of the best pieces of advice the legend has given me … is that if these hate comments go away, maybe you’re not at your peak anymore,” he told Elle. “I think it’s a privilege to be receiving these and rise above it. Ever since she gave me that advice, it’s really changed my perspective and has helped.”

The star is currently on tour in support of his Billboard 200 No. 10 debut album I Barely Know Her, with dates scheduled through summer 2027. The flipper-offer in the crowd in Columbus wasn’t the only unexpected interruption that’s taken place so far on the trek, with sombr taking a pause during his Nov. 3 show in Milwaukee after he chipped his tooth on his water bottle mid-performance.

“Oh, sh–! I chipped my tooth again!” he said at the time. “I’m so happy to inform all of you that ‘Thombr’ has returned.”

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A satellite went knee-deep in the dead, after a voice command from the ground activated the Doom video game in space.

Playing a first-person shooter from 1993 was obviously not in the design plan for the PRETTY cubesat, which is run by a consortium including the European Space Agency (ESA). But the pioneering voice command opens up new worlds for satellite work, the team says.

"Someone in distress at sea or in a remote area could transmit 'mayday' or "help" on a radio," stated Estonia's Tanagra Space, which supplied the software for the feat. The hope is one day, a satellite could use transcription and AI to alert rescue services for assisting folks in remote zones.

The call to play Doom, thankfully, had no other urgency than curiosity — and teamwork, fueled by pizza. OPS-SAT Space Lab managed the experiment on behalf of ESA. Radio amateurs then made six unsuccessful attempts during passes over Poland and Norway, between April and July. The seventh finally reached success under the Oslo Group of the Norwegian Radio Relay League.

"We are radio amateurs, with the emphasis on amateurs. Satellite work was not something our club did, and we had no budget for it," representative Eskil Hadland, call sign LB6AJ, said in the Tangara statement. "So we borrowed a line wrongly credited to Pippi Longstocking: 'I have never tried that before, so I should definitely be able to do that.'"

The Norwegians spent 59 days and about 7200 NOK or $775 (pizza included) to reach PRETTY, helping make changes to the satellite software to pick up a voice. For example, a raw recording of an attempt on July 3, retransmitted to Earth, showed the spoken words to space were unrecognizable. Further work revealed the satellite's receiver channel was too wide to pick up the voice signal, leading to a fix to narrow the channel.

The historic voice command on July 27— in part, "PRETTY play Doom Doom Doom"— came from a rooftop in Oslo, and was spoken at night by Jon Bergli Heier (LB9BJ). PRETTY picked up the transmission, transcribed the command using on-board voice recognition, and then — just like a typical evening gamer—opened up Doom for a play session.

This was no multiplayer gaming situation, but the satellite did create a report of its demon-slaying skills — and its ability to interpret the command. For example, PRETTY generated a "postcard" including a frame of the gameplay, a transcription, and signal diagnostics. The satellite also transmitted its recording of Hadland's command.

As anybody who uses voice-recognition software knows, there are challenges in transcriptions: nobody speaks in exactly the same way, and aspects such as accent or background noise can lead to misinterpretations. The satellite also had to contend with Doppler shift, and with an antenna not designed to relay voices to space.

But the transmission clearly worked, powered by open-source tools including GNU Radio (which handled the signal processing) and Sherpa-ONNX (speech recognition).

The hope is that future spacecraft could one day adapt this approach to radio frequencies for other ideas outside of spoken words. For example, perhaps deep-space radio signals could be detected via satellite, with an AI on board sending the most relevant data to operators after analyzing the work.

For now, however, the Norwegian radio operators are basking in the success: "Our tiny ground station shouted at an ESA spacecraft, and was heard," Hadland said.

#773. Why your physics project needs an anthropologist

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Jaco de Swart is a historian and anthropologist of science at the University of Cambridge, UK.

The TAMBO team assesses suitable observatory sites in the Andes Mountains of Peru.Credit: Jaco de Swart

It is uncommon for a social scientist to have a seat at a meeting about an astronomical observatory, let alone for them to jointly lead one. For one-quarter of attendees to be social-science scholars is almost unprecedented. But that’s exactly what happens at meetings about the Tau Air-shower Mountain-based Observatory (TAMBO), a proposed detector to be built in the Peruvian Andes to look for cosmic particles called tau neutrinos.

Space diplomacy: bridging the operating gaps between myriad missions

Space diplomacy: bridging the operating gaps between myriad missions

Tau neutrinos are elusive fundamental particles that are transmitted through space from black holes and other distant sources. When these particles interact with rocks on Earth, they can produce a shower of other, short-lived particles. The idea behind TAMBO is that if such a shower were emitted from one side of a deep canyon, it could be picked up by an array of 5,000 detectors on the other side (TAMBO collaboration. Nature Astron. 10, 947–951; 2026). The Andes Mountains of Peru contain many promising sites.

For those who live in the area, however, the case for TAMBO is less clear. The Andes are a sensitive ecological environment and home to Indigenous farming communities that consider the mountains sentient beings that are integral to their society. The area is also affected by legal and illegal mining, large-scale infrastructure projects and legacies of colonialism. This all leads to scepticism towards large projects that are developed by people from outside the area.

I am the co-principal investigator of the TAMBO collaboration, alongside Peruvian neutrino physicist Carlos Argüelles at Harvard University in Cambridge, Massachusetts. I lead the social-science and ‘responsible siting’ side of the project. Having received funding to build a proof-of-principle experiment called TAMBITO, we are searching for a potential location for the observatory.

Developing astronomers in Africa: ‘We wanted to create a discipline’

Developing astronomers in Africa: ‘We wanted to create a discipline’

Since 2024, the TAMBO collaboration has built partnerships with 11 Peruvian institutions, which are involved in the design and development of the telescope. Scientific links are an important starting point, but they are not enough. No matter what their discovery potential is, big scientific experiments are not beneficial to everyone. For example, construction of the Thirty Meter Telescope has been stalled since 2015 because of protests triggered by objections to its planned site on Maunakea in Hawaii — a mountain that is sacred in Native Hawaiian culture.

To integrate environmental care into the project and build good relationships with the communities that might host the telescope, TAMBO brought in experts on the Andean region. In 2024, the collaboration held a workshop at Harvard’s Radcliffe Institute for Advanced Study, at which scholars and policymakers discussed what equitable astrophysics in Peru would look like. This led to the formation of a responsible-siting team that includes geographers, sociologists and anthropologists who have worked in the Andes.

CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. — NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman knows how to make an entrance. Under the bright afternoon sun on Saturday (Nov. 7), Isaacman plummeted through the air above 10,000 onlookers, skydiving into the agency's air show MAX POWER.

MAX POWER overtook NASA's Kennedy Space Center here over the weekend, combining aeronautics and aerospace in a massive public air show, the first of its kind for the space agency. A mix of astronauts, fighter jet displays and new technology on display, the spectacle is a lot space-ier than a traditional air show, and Isaacman made sure to really showcase this merging of worlds. A pilot and private astronaut, Jared Isaacman is no stranger to the skies, and immediately after landing back on solid ground he jumped right back up and took to the event's main stage to greet an excited crowd.

"Going into this job, I I knew we had to do something like this," Isaacman said after landing and taking the stage. "We knew on our nation's 250th birthday, we had to open up [the] Kennedy Space Center the year that we returned our astronauts to the lunar environment and put on a little bit of a show."

This mirrorless Canon has specs that make it one of the best cameras available right now, with impressive features and functionality, including a 45MP sensor and excellent high-ISO handling.

Check our in-depth Canon R5 Mark II review.

From thousands of feet above a crowd holding their breath, Isaacman jumped out of a plane alongside members of Skydive Chicago and other notable individuals, including Montana senator Tim Sheehy (R-Montana) and former U.S. Air Force Thunderbird pilot Shawn Gustoson.

One by one, tiny white parachutes popped up in the sky above, which continued to grow in size as the skydivers neared the ground. And before we knew it, Isaacman was gracefully touching down just behind the air show's main stage, landing to the sound of cheers from the eager audience.

In addition to serving in his role as NASA Administrator, Isaacman is an entrepreneur, commercial astronaut and pilot. Known in flight by his callsign "Rook" which he was given during fighter jet training, Isaacman has so far logged over 8,000 flight hours. In 2009, he broke the world record for fastest trip around the world in a light jet (he made the trip in 61 hours, 51 minutes and 15 seconds) and is flight-qualified in a number of military jet aircraft. He also financed and flew on two private orbital space missions on a SpaceX Dragon, Inspiration4 and Polaris Dawn, performing the world's first private spacewalk on the latter misison.

Before jumping out of a plane and careening through the air on Saturday as part of this celebratory stunt, Isaacman was actually flying overhead in not one, but two different fighter jets.

First, he flew an F-5, a lightweight supersonic fighter jet, and just a short while later, Isaacman flew a MiG-29, a twin-engine supersonic fighter jet, over the crowd of excited air show attendees. And the fun didn't stop with this skydive, as Isaacman took to the skies once again, flying over the event in fighter jets on Sunday.

This weekend's MAX POWER events are not a one-time-only celebration of aviation and aerospace at NASA. Earlier in the weekend, the agency announced that in 2028, a week-long event called CAPEWEEK will return to the Kennedy Space Center, promising a next-level showcase of air and space innovation and spectacle.

Isaacman and NASA astronauts presented President Donald Trump, who was onhand for the ceremony, with a gold plaque in his honor that will be installed at the Kennedy Space Center's Shuttle Landing Facility runway in time for the CAPEWEEK in 2028.

"What you are seeing today again, imagine March 2028," Isaacman said of the future. "It's going to be 10x bigger. I mean, not just the the fighter aircraft you're seeing, but displays of aerospace-related hardware, rovers, landers. We're going to bring commercial airliners in here ... I would bet on this, the next new Grand Airliner will be announced here."

"That kind of ambition is exactly that you should expect from your space agency," he added. "I promise you, there'll be more to come."

The new contracts aim to pave the way for a permanent moon base.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. — NASA is pushing ahead with its plan to build a moon base for astronauts by 2032, with the agency unveiling up to $10 billion in contracts to launch and deliver cargo to the moon and other efforts on Saturday (Nov. 7).

The NASA announcement, revealed here during the space agency's "Max Power" air show event at Kennedy Space Center, included plans for a new $10 billion Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) framework, dubbed CLPS 2, about$1.3 billion in funding for the agency's Venture-Class Acquisition of Dedicated and Rideshare (VADR) program, and the nuclear-powered "PROMISE" rover on the moon.

The announcements mark another step in NASA's effort to establish infrastructure on the moon before Artemis astronauts return to its surface, including a rover and other cargo and research elements.

"Under the current CLPS contract, it's all all or nothing, which might be fine if you're only doing one or two of those [missions] per year," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman told Space.com during a press conference on Saturday. "But when you're trying to scale up to what we're talking about today, you want to have the flexibility to move pieces around."

NASA selected eight companies to compete for the new CLPS 2 missions under the framework: Blue Origin, Firefly Aerospace, Intuitive Machines, ispace-U.S., Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, SpaceX and Voyager Technologies.

The contracts for the 10-year CLPS 2 architecture carry a combined maximum value of $10 billion, rather than $10 billion in immediately awarded missions. NASA also increased the ceiling of its existing CLPS contract from $2.6 billion to $4.2 billion to support the agency's "Phase One" Moon Base objectives.

NASA is also following through on a promise Isaacman made in June, when he proposed repurposing an engineering model of the Perseverance and Curiosity Mars rovers (essentially an Earth-based twin) as a mission-ready rover to send to the moon. That rover, called PROMISE (short for "Polar Rover for Observation, Mapping, and In-Situ Exploration"), is a nuclear-powered robot intended to explore the lunar south pole beginning in late 2028.

The autonomous rover will carry a drill and scientific instruments to search for volatiles and water ice on the lunar surface. NASA awarded Blue Origin a $94 million base contract, with an additional $140 million option period based on performance, to deliver PROMISE to the lunar surface aboard its Blue Moon Mark 1 lander.

In addition to that contract for Blue Origin, NASA awarded six launch and orbital transportation task orders worth a total of approximately $1.3 billion to Arrow Science and Technology, Blue Origin and Impulse Space under its Venture-Class Acquisition of Dedicated and Rideshare (VADR) program.

The missions will demonstrate commercial launch and orbital transportation capabilities, including cargo transfers between Earth and lunar orbits, navigation tests with the CAPSTONE 2 spacecraft and lunar scouting with "MoonFall" drones. Blue Origin, SpaceX and Relativity Space will provide launch support with their New Glenn, Falcon 9 and Terran R rockets, respectively.

Under a separate lunar logistics contract, NASA selected SpaceX to launch communications satellites aboard its Starship megarocket in 2028, helping to establish a future lunar communications network with spacecraft similar to the company's Starlink spacecraft.

NASA also awarded contracts to Honeybee Robotics, Redwire and Yank Technologies to develop components for a lunar power and communications tower, known as miniCAST.

The announcements support NASA's Phase One Moon Base strategy, which is scheduled to extend through 2029 and focuses on robotic exploration, infrastructure demonstrations and commercial deliveries. Phase Two, which runs from 2029 to 2032, will continue to build out infrastructure for the base, which will get up and running during Phase 3.

Josh Dinner is Space.com's Spaceflight Staff Writer and a photographer with a passion for science and exploration. He has worked the space beat since 2016, covering the evolution of NASA's commercial spaceflight partnerships and crewed missions, planetary science missions, the Artemis program and humanity's return to the moon. He also enjoys building 1:144-scale model rockets and spacecraft. Find some of Josh's launch photography on Instagram, and follow him on X, where he mostly posts in haiku.
